topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Comparing Lengths & Heights
topic.description: Compare two objects directly by length or height and describe the difference using language such as long, short, tall, longer, shorter, taller, double, half
evidence: Stand two children back-to-back and say who is taller/shorter
Directly compare the heights of two towers and describe one as taller
Use 'longer' and 'shorter' to compare two ribbons placed side by side
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} stands next to the kitchen table and the front door, can they tell you which is taller — and whether they themselves are shorter or taller than each one?

pedagogy.summary: Direct comparison of length or height means putting two objects together and judging which has more — and the whole skill hinges on ALIGNING one endpoint before comparing the other. Length is the distance between an object's two endpoints (CCSS Progression), so a fair comparison needs a common starting line. Children who have not grasped this judge by which object 'sticks out farthest' or by which top is higher, ignoring where each object begins. Back-to-back height comparison is an easy entry because standing on the same floor aligns one endpoint automatically — but that very automaticity hides the alignment move, so it must be made explicit with staggered and raised cases.
bestPractices: Make endpoint alignment the explicit heart of the lesson: line up two objects at a common starting line, THEN compare the far ends
Use a 'mixed-up' puppet (Mr MixUp) who compares without lining up the starting ends, so children catch and correct the endpoint error themselves
Start with back-to-back / side-by-side aligned comparisons, then deliberately stagger the objects and raise one (a tower on a book) so children must attend to the base, not just the top
Build precise comparative language in the moment — longer/shorter, taller/shorter — rather than the global 'bigger'
Address conservation with rotate-and-restore and bend-and-straighten demonstrations: 'it looks longer now, but it really isn't' — show, don't just tell
Give indirect-comparison bridges later (string as a go-between) but keep this stage on fair DIRECT comparison with aligned ends
keyRepresentations: Two ribbons/pencils lined up against a common starting line, far ends compared
A 'mixed-up' puppet placing objects unaligned for the child to fix
Two towers, one raised on a book, prompting attention to a common base
Equal-length strips, one rotated vertical or bent into a curve, to confront non-conservation
commonMisconceptions: Judging by one endpoint — picks the object that 'sticks out farthest' at one end without aligning the starting ends
Ignoring the baseline for height — calls the tower whose top is higher 'taller' even though it stands on a book and has fewer blocks
Non-conservation — believes an object becomes longer when turned vertical, or that a ribbon becomes shorter when curved because its endpoints move closer
Using undifferentiated 'bigger' instead of the specific comparative word (longer/taller), signalling the length attribute is not yet differentiated

learn.summary: Teaches young children (roughly ages 4–6) to compare two objects directly by length or height, with endpoint alignment as the explicit heart of the skill: line up one end at a common starting line, THEN compare the far ends. Addresses the classic errors of judging by whichever end 'sticks out farthest', ignoring a raised baseline for height, and non-conservation (believing length changes when an object is bent or rotated). Builds precise comparative language (longer/shorter, taller/shorter) rather than the global 'bigger'.

activities.title: Line up the ends, then compare (ribbons)
feedback: If the child picks the ribbon poking out while the near ends are unaligned, don't just mark it wrong: have them align the starting ends and look again — because the other (actually longer) ribbon was shifted back, once the starts match it runs further past the finish
Prompt 'where does each one START?' to direct attention to the near endpoints
Use the mixed-up puppet so the child spots and corrects the endpoint error themselves rather than being told
activities.rationale: Length is how far an object extends along itself from one end to the other (for a straight object, from endpoint to endpoint), so a fair direct comparison of two straightened objects needs a common starting line. Children at the Length Direct Comparer level physically align two objects at one endpoint before comparing the others; a mixed-up puppet is a documented way to surface the alignment error. Staggering the pair forces the alignment judgement that a pre-aligned (back-to-back) comparison would do for the child.
sourceClaims: Kindergartners easily compare lengths when objects stand next to each other because that automatically aligns one endpoint (back-to-back height comparison), but in other situations may compare only one endpoint and point to the object that 'sticks out the farthest'; teachers should reinforce the necessity of aligning endpoints (e.g. the pencil-reveal 'were you fooled?'). Length may not be conserved — children may think a stick turned vertical is now longer, or a bent string is now shorter.

At the Length Direct Comparer level a child physically aligns two objects at one endpoint and then compares the other endpoints, using long/longer/longest; instruction focuses on lining objects up at one endpoint before comparing, and notes that in back-to-back height comparison the feet endpoint is aligned for the child so the alignment step often goes unrecognised. A mixed-up puppet is used to surface the endpoint-alignment error.
learnerActions: Look at two ribbons lying staggered on the table, with the SHORTER ribbon shifted so its right end pokes out past the longer ribbon's right end and the near ends left unaligned
Say which ribbon is longer and explain how you know
Either slide both ribbons to a common starting line, or (in a non-draggable image) draw a line to mark the common start, then compare the far ends again
Meet a 'mixed-up' puppet (e.g. Mr MixUp) who compares WITHOUT lining up the starting ends; catch and fix the puppet's mistake
Answer: 'Where does each ribbon START? Put your finger on the beginning of each one.'
activities.intendedInsight: To compare fairly, line up one end of each object at a common start; then the far ends show which is longer. Looking at the far ends tells you nothing reliable while the starting ends are not matched. The object that 'sticks out' at one end is not automatically the longer one.

activities.title: Compare towers from a common base
feedback: If the child says the book-raised tower is taller because its top is higher, guide them to notice it has fewer of the same-sized blocks and starts raised, then bring both to the same surface and compare
Make explicit: 'we compare from where each one STARTS (the base), not just the top'
activities.rationale: Back-to-back/standing comparisons align the base automatically, which hides the alignment move; deliberately raising one object on a book makes the baseline judgement necessary and visible. This parallels endpoint alignment for length, applied to height.
sourceClaims: Kindergartners easily compare lengths when objects stand next to each other because that automatically aligns one endpoint (back-to-back height comparison), but in other situations may compare only one endpoint and point to the object that 'sticks out the farthest'; teachers should reinforce the necessity of aligning endpoints (e.g. the pencil-reveal 'were you fooled?'). Length may not be conserved — children may think a stick turned vertical is now longer, or a bent string is now shorter.
learnerActions: Look at two towers built from identical blocks: a taller tower (more blocks) standing on the floor, and a shorter tower (fewer blocks) standing on a thick book so its TOP is higher
Say which tower is taller and explain how you know
Bring the book-raised tower down onto the floor (or reason explicitly about the book's height) so both start from the same surface, then compare again
Try a harder case: raise the shorter tower even higher on two books — 'now is it taller? What if I put it on the floor?'
activities.intendedInsight: To compare heights fairly, both objects must start from a common base; you cannot judge just by where the tops are. Here the shorter tower looks taller only because it sits on a book; move both to the same surface to compare fairly.

activities.title: Does length change when you bend it? (conservation)
feedback: If the child says the straight ribbon is now longer than the curved one, do NOT mark it wrong or drill it: narrate 'it looks longer now, but it really isn't', straighten the ribbon, and let them check
Let the child predict first, then restore the shape to confirm — show, don't just tell
activities.rationale: Non-conservation of length is developmental: children may judge length by how far apart the endpoints look, so a curved ribbon seems shorter and a vertical stick seems longer. Conservation emerges with maturation and experience, so repeated predict-then-check bend-and-straighten / rotate-and-restore demonstrations are more appropriate than correction or drilling.
sourceClaims: Kindergartners easily compare lengths when objects stand next to each other because that automatically aligns one endpoint (back-to-back height comparison), but in other situations may compare only one endpoint and point to the object that 'sticks out the farthest'; teachers should reinforce the necessity of aligning endpoints (e.g. the pencil-reveal 'were you fooled?'). Length may not be conserved — children may think a stick turned vertical is now longer, or a bent string is now shorter.
learnerActions: Look at two ribbons of exactly equal length; one is then bent into a wavy curve
Predict: 'are they still the same length, or is one longer now?'
Watch (or press 'straighten') as the curved ribbon is straightened back out, and check the prediction
Try the rotate version: an equal stick turned vertical — predict whether it 'got longer', then restore it to compare
activities.intendedInsight: Length does not change just because an object is bent or turned — a bent ribbon is the same length when straightened; a stick is the same length lying down or standing up (though how tall it stands does depend on which way it is turned).

activities.title: Say it precisely: longer, shorter, taller
feedback: If the child points to the correct object but calls it 'bigger', name the specific attribute and its comparative word tied to the length/height question before more practice
Gently correct loose mixing of longer/shorter/taller by tying each word to what is being compared
activities.rationale: Using undifferentiated 'bigger' signals the length attribute is not yet separated from global size; KS1 expectations include comparing and describing lengths and heights with vocabulary such as long/short, longer/shorter, tall/short. Building the comparative word in the moment of comparison supports attribute differentiation.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils should compare, describe and solve practical problems for lengths and heights and measure lengths/heights, using vocabulary such as long/short, longer/shorter, tall/short, double/half.
learnerActions: After each comparison, describe the result with the specific comparative word — 'this ribbon is LONGER', 'this tower is TALLER' — not just 'bigger'
Match the word to the attribute: longer/shorter for length laid out, taller/shorter for height standing up
Describe practical real-object pairs (two pencils, two strips) using long/short, longer/shorter, tall/short
activities.intendedInsight: Length and height are specific attributes with specific words; naming them precisely shows you are comparing the right thing, not just overall 'size'.

constraints: Pre-aligned comparisons (back-to-back, side-by-side at a common start) can be passed WITHOUT understanding, because the alignment is done for the child; include staggered pairs and a raised tower so the child must perform the alignment/baseline judgement.

A static picture or tap-to-reveal image can show aligned vs unaligned pairs and reveal the correct answer, but the child does not physically slide objects into alignment — the core action is demonstrated rather than done. Treat such images as a scaffold toward hands-on or draggable aligning.

A recognition-only selection task ('which is longer?') scores the alignment judgement but does not let the child perform the physical align action with live feedback — recognition alone does not elicit the aligning action; a draw-a-line-to-align step adds a construction element, though still short of free manipulation.
Non-conservation is developmental: do not mark it wrong or drill it. Provide repeated predict-then-check demonstrations and let conservation emerge with experience.
Keep this stage on fair DIRECT comparison with aligned ends; indirect-comparison bridges (e.g. using a string as a go-between) belong to a later stage.
Build precise comparative language (longer/shorter, taller/shorter) rather than the global 'bigger'.

Real objects have thickness and sit on surfaces; the alignment idea is about the endpoints/base. When using an on-screen model, treat it as a representation of the physical lining-up action, not a replacement for it where hands-on tools are expected.
Double/half language appears in the curriculum statement but is beyond simple direct comparison; introduce only when ready and do not conflate it with longer/shorter judgements.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The original flagged the UK National Curriculum (KS1) source as unverified (verified:false); treat the double/half and vocabulary claim accordingly.

The source row's artefact-fit notes asserted that a 3D back-to-back view 'adds little' and that a conversation 'cannot render' the comparison. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established efficacy claims; retained only as scope observations, not universal laws. A spoken/role interaction could still support reasoning aloud even if it does not itself provide the object to align.

Optional interactive mechanisms from the original design (drag two ribbons to a start line; a near-end alignment marker; far-end comparison that 'lights up' only when aligned; a Mr MixUp mode; slide-tower-off-a-book; a 'straighten' button for the conservation case) are preserved as example feedback mechanisms, not mandatory requirements.

One misconception (undifferentiated 'bigger') links to a prerequisite micro-topic on the underlying attribute distinction; reteaching that attribute distinction may be needed before precise-vocabulary practice.

The LearningTrajectories 'Length Direct Comparer' claim supports endpoint alignment (activities 1 and 2) but does not address conservation; it is therefore attached only to the alignment activity and excluded from the conservation activity's sourceClaims, which rests on the CCSS conservation statement only.

probeDeeper: 'Where does each ribbon START? Put your finger on the beginning of each one.' (surfaces whether the child attends to the near endpoints)
Counterexample: raise the SHORTER tower even higher on two books — 'now is it taller? What if I put it on the floor?' (tests baseline reasoning against a stronger illusion)
'You said this straight one is longer than the curly one. Watch — I'll straighten the curly one. Now which is longer?' (confronts non-conservation with a restore)
'Show me a fair way to check which of these two pencils is longer.' (checks the child can set up aligned direct comparison independently)
assess.correctAnswer: (1) Lines up one end of both ribbons at a common starting line, then compares the far ends, and names the genuinely longer ribbon (not the one that was poking out). (2) Compares from a common base — recognises the book-raised tower only looks taller, brings both to the same surface or reasons about the book's height, and identifies the tower with more actual height. (3) Says the two ribbons are still the same length even though one is now curved — length is conserved when a ribbon is bent.

responseLevels.gap: Judges by a single protruding end or by which top is higher regardless of the base; cannot reliably line objects up; believes length changes when a ribbon is bent.
responseLevels.full: Spontaneously aligns one endpoint (or equalises the base) before comparing the far ends across staggered and raised cases, holds length invariant under rotation and bending, and describes the result with precise comparative language (longer/shorter/taller).
responseLevels.partial: Compares correctly when objects are already side by side at a common start (back-to-back), but is fooled by staggered ribbons or a raised tower, and/or does not yet conserve length under bending/rotation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set three tasks and WATCH — do not explain the method first. (1) Lay two ribbons of different lengths on the table STAGGERED: shift the SHORTER ribbon forward so its far end sticks out past the longer one's far end, and leave the near ends unaligned. Ask 'which ribbon is longer? Show me how you know.' (2) Build two block towers — one taller tower on the floor, and a shorter tower standing on a thick book so its TOP is higher. Ask 'which tower is taller?' (3) Take two ribbons of exactly equal length; bend one into a wavy curve. Ask 'are they still the same length, or is one longer now?' Watch whether the child aligns the starting ends, accounts for the raised base, and conserves length.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Pre-aligned comparisons (back-to-back) can be passed without understanding, because the alignment is done for the child. Staggering the ribbons and raising one tower forces the alignment/baseline judgement: a child who judges by a single protruding end picks the shorter ribbon, and one who judges by 'highest top' picks the raised tower — both tells. The conservation item separates children who believe length changes with shape from those who hold it invariant.

topic.name: Measuring mass and weight (age 4+)
topic.description: Compare two objects directly by mass or weight and describe the difference using language such as heavy, light, heavier than, lighter than
evidence: Heft two objects and say which is heavier/lighter
Use a simple balance to compare the weight of two objects
Describe one object as 'heavier than' another
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} holds a bag of apples in one hand and a feather in the other, can they tell you which is heavier and use words like "much heavier than" to describe the difference?

pedagogy.summary: Children compare which of two objects is heavier by HEFTING (holding one in each hand) and by using a two-pan balance, learning that weight is felt and measured, not seen — size and appearance do not reliably tell you mass. The balance settles cases hefting can't. Language: heavy/light, heavier than, lighter than. (At this stage 'mass' and 'weight' are used interchangeably.)
bestPractices: Heft first (hands as scales), then confirm with a balance
Deliberately pair a small heavy object with a big light one so size cannot decide it — this is what breaks the 'bigger = heavier' assumption
Read the balance as 'the side that goes DOWN is heavier'
Use full comparative sentences: 'the tin is heavier than the box'
Keep it practical with real objects; move to ordering three items by pairwise balance comparisons
keyRepresentations: The two-pan balance (canonical model of comparison)
Hands as scales (hefting)
Deliberately mismatched pairs (small-heavy vs big-light)
commonMisconceptions: Bigger = heavier — judges mass by size or appearance
The taller/longer/fuller object is heavier (conflates mass with another attribute)
Misreads the balance — thinks the RAISED pan is the heavier side
Expects to order objects by weight just by looking

learn.summary: Young children (about 4-6) compare which of two objects is heavier, first by HEFTING (holding one object in each hand) and then by confirming with a two-pan balance. The central aim is to challenge the 'bigger = heavier' assumption by deliberately pairing a small heavy object with a big light one, so size stops being a reliable guide. Children read the balance as 'the side that goes DOWN is heavier', use full comparative language (heavier than / lighter than), and progress to ordering three objects by pairwise comparison. At this stage 'mass' and 'weight' are used interchangeably. The curriculum frames this as a practical activity with real materials; screen or picture activities can support balance-reading and prediction but cannot deliver the felt sense of weight (no haptics).

activities.title: Heft then balance: feel it, then confirm
feedback: If the child picks the larger object, invite them to heft the pair with eyes shut, then let the balance decide — evidence over appearance. Repeat with more small-heavy/big-light pairs so size is repeatedly wrong.

If the child reads the balance backwards (raised pan = heavier), model with a known heavy-vs-light pair so they watch the heavy side drop; say 'the heavier side pushes DOWN' and let them press a pan to feel it fall.
When correct, prompt the reasoning: 'This one is smaller but you said it's heavier — how can something small be heavy?'
activities.rationale: For this age the embodied experience of feeling a small object press down is intended to do the conceptual work of challenging 'bigger = heavier'; the balance then provides shared, visible evidence that overrides appearance. The curriculum frames comparison of mass as a practical activity with real materials, moving from feeling to a balance.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils are taught to compare, describe and solve practical problems for mass/weight [heavy/light, heavier than, lighter than] and to 'measure and begin to record' mass/weight; at this stage mass and weight are used interchangeably.

NCETM Year 1 mastery mass tasks move from feeling ('sort three items lightest to heaviest by feeling them') to a balance with items 'quite similar in mass', and probe balance-reasoning ('which is heavier?', 'if you added a car to the teddy what would happen to the scales?', true/false from a balance picture) — designed so appearance/feel is unreliable and balance evidence decides.
Measurement Big Ideas frame it as comparison and equivalence conducted as a practical activity with real materials.
learnerActions: Hold one object in each hand (heft) and say which feels heavier — try this with eyes shut so appearance can't guide the choice.

Pair a small heavy object (a metal weight or pebble) with a big light object (an empty plastic box or inflated balloon), checked beforehand on the balance so the small item really is heavier (a small pebble can be lighter than a large box). Predict which is heavier before touching.
Place both on a two-pan balance and watch which pan goes down; say 'the ____ is heavier than the ____' in a full sentence.
Repeat with several deliberately misleading pairs (e.g. big cushion vs small tin of beans), checked beforehand so the small item really is heavier, so that size is repeatedly the wrong guide.
Press gently on one pan with a hand to feel that pushing down harder on one side makes that pan go down, just as a heavier object does.
activities.intendedInsight: Weight is felt and measured, not seen — a small object can be heavier than a big one, and the balance settles cases your eyes cannot.

activities.title: Order three objects by weight
feedback: If the child orders by look or by trial-and-error grabbing, scaffold with pairwise balance comparisons ('heavier than this one? lighter than that one?'). Systematic seriation is not expected at this age — it consolidates with practice, so do not drill an ordering rule.
Praise reasoning that uses the balance evidence to justify each placement.
activities.rationale: Ordering by successive pairwise balancing extends direct comparison and reinforces that weight evidence, not appearance, decides order. Developmentally, systematic seriation emerges gradually, so the task is scaffolded rather than drilled.
sourceClaims: NCETM Year 1 mastery mass tasks move from feeling ('sort three items lightest to heaviest by feeling them') to a balance with items 'quite similar in mass', and probe balance-reasoning ('which is heavier?', 'if you added a car to the teddy what would happen to the scales?', true/false from a balance picture) — designed so appearance/feel is unreliable and balance evidence decides.
Measurement Big Ideas frame it as comparison and equivalence conducted as a practical activity with real materials.
learnerActions: Take three objects, including at least one small-heavy and one big-light item.
Compare them two at a time on the balance ('Is this heavier than that?'), using the balance outcome each time.
Arrange them lightest to heaviest based on the pairwise comparisons, not on how they look.
Describe the order aloud using 'heavier than' and 'lighter than'.
activities.intendedInsight: You can put objects in order of weight by comparing pairs, and the order may differ from what their sizes suggest.

activities.title: Virtual balance: predict then watch the beam tip (scaffold)
feedback: When a prediction is wrong, replay the beam tipping and point out which labelled side went down.
Use the misleading pairs to prompt: 'It looked bigger — why did the other side drop?'
activities.rationale: A predict-then-reveal virtual balance may support balance-reading, prediction and the size-vs-weight surprise. It is offered as a scaffold: a screen cannot deliver the physical heft that is how young children first feel that weight isn't size, so it should supplement, not replace, hands-on work. The outcome is designer-controlled, so the objects must be configured so the small item really is heavier.
sourceClaims: NCETM Year 1 mastery mass tasks move from feeling ('sort three items lightest to heaviest by feeling them') to a balance with items 'quite similar in mass', and probe balance-reasoning ('which is heavier?', 'if you added a car to the teddy what would happen to the scales?', true/false from a balance picture) — designed so appearance/feel is unreliable and balance evidence decides.
learnerActions: Drag a small metal cube and a big foam block onto the two pans of a virtual two-pan balance; the objects are configured so the small dense cube genuinely outweighs the larger light block.
Predict which side will drop before releasing.
Watch the beam tip to reveal that the small cube wins, with running 'heavier/lighter' labels appearing on each side.
Try a round of deliberately misleading pairs (big cushion vs small tin), again set so the small heavy item is actually heavier.
Switch to an order-three-objects mode that works by successive balancing.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a balance (down = heavier) and predicting outcomes can be practised on screen, and in this set-up (where the small object is actually heavier) the small-cube-wins surprise reinforces that size alone is not a reliable guide to weight.

activities.title: Balance-picture check (recognition)
feedback: If a child names the raised side as heavier, return to a real or virtual balance and watch the heavier side drop.
For true/false items, ask the child to point to which pan is down to justify their answer.
activities.rationale: Picture-based items give clean checks of balance-reading and comparison. They check interpretation (recognition) and do not elicit the child's own physical comparison; hefting cannot be assessed from a picture, so use these to confirm interpretation alongside hands-on work rather than in place of it.
sourceClaims: NCETM Year 1 mastery mass tasks move from feeling ('sort three items lightest to heaviest by feeling them') to a balance with items 'quite similar in mass', and probe balance-reasoning ('which is heavier?', 'if you added a car to the teddy what would happen to the scales?', true/false from a balance picture) — designed so appearance/feel is unreliable and balance evidence decides.
learnerActions: Look at a picture of a two-pan balance and say which object is heavier (the side tipped down).
Order a set of objects lightest-to-heaviest from a series of balance pictures.
Match objects to the balance outcome they would produce.
Answer a true/false claim read from a balance picture (e.g. 'the teddy is heavier than the car').
activities.intendedInsight: Once the physical idea is in place, you can interpret balance pictures: the lower pan holds the heavier object.

constraints: The curriculum frames this as a practical activity with real objects in real hands: hefting a small heavy object and feeling it press down is the embodied experience intended to challenge 'bigger = heavier'. Screen and picture activities can point toward this but cannot supply the felt sense of weight (no haptics).

Deliberately include at least one small-heavy vs big-light pair, and ensure the chosen materials really do make the small item heavier — this mismatch is what makes size an unreliable guide; without it the activity can be solved by appearance alone.
Virtual-balance and balance-picture tasks are scaffolds for balance-reading and prediction; they do not assess or supply the felt sense of heft, so pair them with hands-on comparison.
Recognition-only picture tasks (choosing/matching) check interpretation but do not elicit the child's own physical comparison; do not rely on them as the only evidence of understanding.
Do not expect systematic ordering (seriation) of three objects at this age; scaffold with pairwise comparisons and let it consolidate with practice rather than drilling a rule.
Read the balance explicitly as 'the side that goes DOWN is heavier' (if the pans stay level, the objects weigh the same) and watch for the common reversal (thinking the raised pan is heavier).
Use full comparative sentences ('the tin is heavier than the box') rather than single words.
'Mass' and 'weight' are treated interchangeably at this stage; this is an age-appropriate simplification, not a claim that they are the same quantity.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row asserted a 3D balance 'adds nothing' over 2D and that a dialogue 'cannot' let a child heft or balance objects. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened: a 3D model and in-role dialogue simply offer different affordances and neither provides real heft; the genuine objective limit is that screens and pictures cannot deliver the felt sense of weight.

Efficacy wording was softened throughout (e.g. 'intended to', 'may support'): the pedagogical value of hefting and the virtual balance for this age is plausible and curriculum-aligned but not empirically validated here.

The virtual 'small cube wins' result is only true for suitably chosen sizes/densities; a large enough foam block could outweigh a tiny metal cube. Because the virtual balance is designer-controlled, the objects should be configured so the small item is genuinely heavier; for real objects, pick a clearly dense small item against a clearly light large item.
'Mass and weight used interchangeably' is a pedagogical simplification for ages 4-6; it is scientifically imprecise but appropriate here and flagged as such.

'Here's a big cushion and a small tin of beans — which is heavier? How could you be SURE?' (a fresh big-light vs small-heavy case)
'When they're on the balance, how do you know which side is the heavier one?'
assess.correctAnswer: Hefts and reports the small metal object as heavier despite being smaller (it presses down); on the balance names the pan that goes DOWN as the heavier one; orders the three by weight (not by size), using 'heavier than / lighter than'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges the heavier object by size or appearance — 'the big box must be heavier because it's bigger'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have them heft the pair with eyes shut, then let the balance settle it — evidence over appearance; repeat with several small-heavy / big-light pairs so size is repeatedly wrong.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 1 picks the larger object before or against hefting; discounts the balance when it contradicts size

errorPatterns.nextMove: Model with a known heavy vs light pair so they watch the heavy side drop; 'the heavier side pushes DOWN'; let them press a pan to feel it fall.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a small heavy object (a metal weight or a pebble) and a large light object (a big empty plastic box or an inflated balloon), plus a third object, and a two-pan balance. (3) 'Put all three in order, lightest to heaviest.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The deliberately small-heavy vs big-light pairing IS the discriminator — a child relying on size says the big box is heavier, a child attending to weight says the metal object is; the balance item separately catches whether they read 'down = heavier'.

pedagogy.summary: Year-1 children make the leap from comparing lengths to quantifying them: laying identical units (cubes, paper clips) end to end and counting them, then beginning to read a centimetre ruler. The concept underneath the procedure is that a measurement is a count of equal-sized length-units tiling the object with no gaps or overlaps, always recorded as a number WITH a unit.
bestPractices: Begin with non-standard units (interlocking cubes, paper clips) laid end to end; count and record the result before any ruler is introduced.
Insist the units are identical in size — deliberately contrast a row measured with mixed-size units so children see why equal units matter.
Make iteration self-checking: units abut with no gaps and no overlaps; have children build their own paper ruler by marking off one repeated unit, tying the ruler back to iteration.
Always attach a unit to the number ('8 cubes', '12 cm') and ask 'what are you counting?' so the number stays tied to length, not to how many objects.
Introduce the centimetre ruler as a tool that simply counts the same iterated units, with the start of the object aligned to the beginning of the ruler.

commonMisconceptions: Leaves gaps between units or overlaps them, treating measuring as 'placing things along' rather than covering the length.
Uses mixed-size units yet counts them as one total.
Counts the number of discrete objects (cardinality) rather than the length covered — e.g. a row of 6 short matches is called 'longer' than an equal row of 5 longer matches.
Begins counting the ruler at the numeral '1' instead of the zero/start.

The core concept is that a measurement is a count of equal-sized length-units tiling the object completely, always recorded as a number WITH a unit.

activities.title: Tile the length with identical cubes
feedback: If there is a gap between cubes, run a finger along the uncovered stretch and ask: is that length being counted? Close the gap and re-count.
If two cubes overlap, point out that the same stretch is being counted twice; separate them so they just abut.
When the row is clean and gap-free, confirm the count and always restate it with the unit: 'about 8 cubes long.'

In a digital version the running counter can redden or refuse to total a gappy or overlapping row, and only count a cleanly tiled row — so the no-gaps/no-overlaps rule is felt, not just told. This live recompute is one optional way to make the rule self-checking.
activities.rationale: Year-1 children often slide units without abutting them exactly and are not concerned about accuracy, so self-checking iteration (abutting units, finger-check, or a recompute that only counts a clean row) targets the actual procedural leap of covering the length rather than merely placing units along it.
sourceClaims: Measuring length means iterating a chosen unit end to end with no gaps or overlaps and counting the units; Grade 1 children may initially leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering the length; units must be the same size; children may count discrete objects (cardinality) and call a row with more, smaller items 'longer'; a measurement is a number assigned relative to a unit and must be recorded with its unit.

In the Length Unit Relater and Repeater level children iterate a single unit and understand the need for equal-length units; children often are not concerned about accuracy when iterating (sliding a unit without abutting it exactly), so the best activities are self-checking.
learnerActions: Place a pencil or book in front of you and a tub of same-size cubes beside it.
Lay cube after cube along the pencil, end to end, from one end of the pencil.
Nudge the cubes so each one touches the next with no gaps and no overlaps.
Count the cubes and say the result as a number with its unit, e.g. '8 cubes'.
Run a finger along the pencil to check no uncovered stretch is left between cubes.
activities.intendedInsight: A length-count only means the length when identical units cover the object completely, with no gaps and no overlaps.

activities.title: Why the units must all be the same size
feedback: If the child counts mixed sizes as one total, pause on the '3 large and 4 small' challenge: are these 7 of the same thing? Establish that the units must all match before the count means anything.
After re-measuring with one size, confirm the total and connect it back to the clean, equal-unit row.
Ask 'would bigger units give you more or fewer?' to check they expect a larger unit to give a smaller count.
activities.rationale: Deliberately contrasting equal versus mixed units exposes the equal-unit rule directly; this addresses the documented misconception of counting mixed-size units as a single total.

In the Length Unit Relater and Repeater level children iterate a single unit and understand the need for equal-length units; children often are not concerned about accuracy when iterating (sliding a unit without abutting it exactly), so the best activities are self-checking.
learnerActions: Measure the book again, but this time use a bin that has a few oversized blocks mixed in with the small cubes.
Report the total and check whether it makes sense.
Try the challenge: '3 large blocks and 4 small blocks laid in a row — is the book 7 blocks long?' Explain your answer.
Re-measure the book using only one size of unit and compare.
activities.intendedInsight: A measurement is only meaningful when every unit is the same size; mixing sizes makes the count nonsense.

activities.title: Length is extent, not how many pieces
feedback: If the child says the 6-match row is longer because it has more pieces, lay the two rows side by side aligned at one end so they can see whether the extents match.
When asked 'what are you counting?', steer from 'the matches' toward 'the length' — the number of pieces alone does not tell you the length unless the pieces are the same size.
If the child lines the rows up and finds they reach the same point, confirm they are the same length and ask how aligning at one end let them tell.
activities.rationale: Children often judge length by cardinality, calling a row of more, smaller items 'longer'. The two rows are set up to be the same total length (an off-stage setup condition the child is not told); direct side-by-side comparison re-anchors length as extent independent of the number of pieces.
sourceClaims: Measuring length means iterating a chosen unit end to end with no gaps or overlaps and counting the units; Grade 1 children may initially leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering the length; units must be the same size; children may count discrete objects (cardinality) and call a row with more, smaller items 'longer'; a measurement is a number assigned relative to a unit and must be recorded with its unit.
learnerActions: Look at two rows of matches: one row made of 6 short matches and one row made of 5 longer matches.
Decide which row is longer, or whether they are the same length, and say what you are counting.
Lay the two rows directly side by side, aligned at one end, to check your answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Length is how far something extends, not how many pieces make up the row; more pieces does not mean longer.

activities.title: Build a paper ruler and read a centimetre ruler
feedback: If the child lines the object up with '1', show that the stretch from 0 to '1' is already one unit, so reading the numeral at the far end gives one centimetre too many; realign to 0 and re-read.
If they read off the last numeral the object touches without aligning the start, go back to the paper ruler to re-connect numerals to counted units.
Confirm the recorded result always carries its unit ('15 cm'), not a bare number.
In a digital version a virtual ruler can be required to align at 0 before it reads out, linking the tiled units to the tool. This is one optional way to make the zero-start concrete.
activities.rationale: Building a paper ruler from a single repeated unit ties the ruler back to iteration, and keeps ruler work light at this age. Starting at '1' or reading the last numeral touched are common Year-1 errors the zero-alignment work addresses.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils measure and begin to record lengths and heights using non-standard and then standard units, and begin to use a ruler.

Measuring length means iterating a chosen unit end to end with no gaps or overlaps and counting the units; Grade 1 children may initially leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering the length; units must be the same size; children may count discrete objects (cardinality) and call a row with more, smaller items 'longer'; a measurement is a number assigned relative to a unit and must be recorded with its unit.
learnerActions: Take a strip of paper and mark off one chosen unit over and over, end to end, to make your own ruler.
Use your paper ruler to measure a short object, counting the units.
Now take a centimetre ruler and line its start (the 0) up with one end of the object, not the '1' mark.
Read off how many centimetres long the object is and record it as a number with its unit, e.g. '15 cm'.
activities.intendedInsight: A ruler is just a tool that counts the same iterated units; you start from zero because the numerals name the units of space already covered.

activities.title: Spot-the-gap and how-many checks
feedback: For a 'spot the gappy row' choice, name exactly what is wrong with each rejected row — a gap, an overlap, or mixed-size units.
For a how-many answer that is off by one, check where the count started: for a cube row, the first cube is counted as 1; for a ruler picture, the object should start at the 0 mark.
Use these as checks after hands-on practice, not instead of it.
activities.rationale: Recognition items and sliders can check the idea and a spot-the-gap step is discriminating, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the hand-action of building a clean row; keep these as post-practice checks.
learnerActions: Look at several pictured rows and pick which one has been measured correctly (no gaps, no overlaps, equal units).
For a tidy row of cubes, say or set a slider to how many cubes long it is.
For a ruler picture, say how many centimetres long the object is.
activities.intendedInsight: You can recognise a correctly measured row and read a count, but recognising one does not by itself build the skill of producing a clean row yourself.

constraints: Begin with non-standard units (interlocking cubes, paper clips) laid end to end; count and record before any ruler is introduced.
Always attach a unit to the number ('8 cubes', '12 cm') and ask 'what are you counting?' so the number stays tied to length, not to how many objects.
Keep ruler work light at this age; a child-made paper ruler tying the ruler back to a single repeated unit is the bridge to the centimetre ruler.

Recognition/selection items (spot-the-gap, how-many sliders) check understanding but do not by themselves build the hand-action of iterating and fixing a gappy row; use them as post-practice checks, not the main activity.

A static tap-to-reveal of a cube-row or ruler ('each cube = one length-unit', '0 starts here') can clarify the meaning of the marks as a reference, but a fixed image cannot be re-tiled by the child; pair it with hands-on or interactive iteration.

Physical cubes and an on-screen model offer different experiences; neither is claimed as the only way to learn iteration. Prefer whichever lets the child iterate units and get honest feedback on gaps, overlaps and mixed sizes.
When probing cardinality-vs-length, present or compare rows by aligning the objects side by side at one end; reteaching may require returning to direct length comparison as a prerequisite.

The matches example only demonstrates cardinality-vs-length if the two rows are genuinely the same total length; set the rows to be physically equal but do NOT tell the child they are equal, so the comparison stays open and is discovered by aligning them.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated 3D as 'poor' because length is one-dimensional, and dialogue/conversation as 'poor' for a procedural skill. These catalog fit-rankings are not retained as universal pedagogical laws; the relevant objective limit (recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction) is kept, but claims that a static image or a conversation 'cannot teach' are softened or dropped.
The UK National Curriculum source is marked verified:false in the row; treat the Year-1 ruler claim accordingly.

Self-audit of the matches example: a row of 6 shorter matches and a row of 5 longer matches must be set to the same total length to illustrate cardinality-vs-length. This equality is a setup condition kept off-stage; the child-facing prompt no longer states the rows are equal (that would give away the answer) and instead offers 'same length' as one allowed answer the child can reach by aligning the rows.

Self-audit of ruler logic: aligning the object end with 0 (not '1') is correct — the space before the '1' mark is already one unit — so reading from '1' loses a unit; this correction is retained in the activity.

Corrected the cardinality activity on independent review: the prior feedback 'end to end' (which joins rows lengthwise) was already changed to side-by-side alignment, and the learner-facing setup that revealed the rows as 'the same total length' has now been removed so the probe is neither leading nor self-answering; the equality remains only as an off-stage setup condition in the constraints and rationale.

probeDeeper: You said 8 — 8 what? Point to one of them.
If I measured this same book with these bigger blocks instead, would I get more than 8 or fewer than 8? Why?
Watch — I'll lay them like this (place with a gap). Is that measuring properly? What's wrong with it?
Can you start the ruler somewhere other than the end and still get the right length?
assess.correctAnswer: The child lays identical units end to end from one end of the book with no gaps or overlaps, counts the length-units (not the objects at random), states and records the count WITH a unit ('about 12 cubes' / '15 cm'), and — when they reach for the ruler — aligns its start (0) with the end of the book rather than the '1' mark.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gaps or overlaps: lays units with spaces between them or overlapping, as if measuring is 'putting things along' the object rather than covering its whole length with no holes.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach in place: have them run a finger along the object to feel the uncovered length between cubes; use abutting, self-checking units and re-count.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cubes placed with visible gaps or overlapping; the child still counts them and offers a number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mixed-size units counted as equal: combines cubes and larger blocks and reports one total, not noticing the units differ.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pose the '3 large blocks and 4 small blocks — is it 7 blocks long?' challenge; establish that measuring units must all be the same size, then re-measure with one size.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A row of different-sized objects counted as a single number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts discrete objects, not length (cardinality): judges length by how many pieces there are, so a row of more, smaller units is called 'longer' than an equal-length row of fewer, larger units.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the matches-experiment discussion and to direct length comparison so length is re-anchored as extent independent of the number of pieces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Shown two equal-length rows, the child says the one with more items is longer; answers 'what are you counting?' with 'the cubes' not 'the length'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ruler read from '1': treats the numerals as signals for where to start counting, so lines the book up with the '1' mark or reports the last numeral touched.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that 0 is the start and that a numeral names the units of space already covered; keep ruler work light at this age and build a paper ruler by iterating a single unit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Object aligned to the '1' on the ruler, or the final numeral crossed read off as the length; answer off by one.

responseLevels.gap: Lays units with gaps/overlaps or mixes sizes, or gives a bare number with no unit, or judges length by how many pieces there are regardless of the actual extent.
responseLevels.full: Lays identical units with no gaps or overlaps from one end, counts the length-units, records the number with its unit, aligns the ruler's zero, and can say a bigger unit would give a smaller count.
responseLevels.partial: Lays equal units end to end and counts them, but the procedure is fragile: e.g. iterates cubes cleanly yet starts the ruler at '1', or omits the unit unless prompted — succeeds in the practised case but does not transfer to the ruler.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set out a book, a tub of same-size cubes with a few larger blocks mixed in, and a centimetre ruler. Say: 'Measure how long this book is and tell me the number.' Do not tell them how. Watch how they lay the units, whether they mix sizes, and where they start the ruler; then ask them to write the result down.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the concept produces a clean, gap-free row of equal units and a number-with-unit, and starts the ruler at zero. A child who lacks it reveals precisely which sub-idea is missing in the way they lay and read — gaps/overlaps, mixed units, counting objects, or starting at 1 — none of which a child with the full concept does. The performance is watched, never asked about.

Insist units are identical — mixing cube sizes breaks the count (the unit-size principle: a larger unit gives a smaller count)
When reading a dial/scale, first work out what one interval is worth, then count intervals (spaces) to the pointer, not the marks
Estimate first, then check by measuring
Keep it practical; wait for the balance beam to settle before reading

Dial / kitchen scale with graduations
The number-line-like scale of graduations
The record: '5 cubes' or '200 g'

learn.summary: Children move from comparing mass to quantifying it: expressing mass as a number of units — first non-standard (this book balances 5 cubes), then standard (grams, kilograms) — and reading a simple dial or scale. A balance shows equivalence (the object balances N identical units); reading a graduated scale means valuing the intervals, not counting marks. The key insight is that a larger unit gives a smaller count for the same object.

activities.title: Balance it with identical units
feedback: If a count is reported while the beam is still moving, prompt: wait for the beam to settle, then read. If it settles tipped to one side, it is not balanced, so add or remove a cube; if no whole number of cubes levels it exactly, record 'about' or 'between' two counts.
If cubes of mixed sizes were used, point out that the count only means something when every unit is identical; redo with one size.
If the estimate was far off, that is fine — the point is to compare your estimate with the measured count and notice the gap.
activities.rationale: Equivalence via balancing is a concrete route into quantifying mass and underpins later standard-unit work. Recording as number-plus-unit anchors the idea that the unit matters.
sourceClaims: NCETM mastery tasks assess mass via balance equivalence ('this box weighs 10 kg, how much does each tin weigh?') and via reading dial/kitchen scales to compare masses ('what is the mass of two red bags? which is heavier, red or green? explain'); the Year 1 Big Idea introduces equivalence ('how many cubes are equivalent to the mass of the teddy?').
learnerActions: Place a book (or other object) on one pan of a balance.

Add identical unit-weights (e.g. interlocking cubes) one at a time to the other pan until the beam levels, or is as near level as you can get; if one more cube tips it the other way, the object is between two counts.

Wait for the beam to settle before reading, then count the cubes and record the result as a number with its unit, e.g. '8 cubes', or 'about 8 cubes' / 'between 8 and 9 cubes' if it never quite levels.
Before you start adding cubes, check every cube is the same size; set aside any odd-sized ones.
Before adding any cubes, estimate how many you expect; after measuring, compare your estimate with the measured count.
activities.intendedInsight: Mass can be quantified as a number of identical units that balance the object; the record is a number plus a unit, not just a number.

activities.title: Same book, different unit size
feedback: If the child says the smaller big-cube count means the book is now lighter or has changed, show one big cube balancing several small cubes, so one big = many small; then the smaller count for the same book makes sense.
If the child claims 15 small cubes is heavier than 10 big cubes just because 15 > 10, compare the actual units directly on the balance: you cannot compare counts made with different-sized units.
Correct reasoning to reinforce: 'bigger cubes are heavier, so fewer of them balance the same book'.
activities.rationale: Directly targets unit-size ignorance by letting the child watch the count drop for an unchanged object. The inverse relationship between unit size and count is a core measurement idea, and discrete counting can otherwise convince children that unit size is irrelevant.
sourceClaims: The larger the unit, the fewer units in a given measurement (inverse relationship between unit size and count); counting discrete items can wrongly convince children that unit size doesn't matter, when in measurement it is critical.
learnerActions: Measure the SAME book again, this time using larger unit-weights.
Count how many large units balance the book and compare with the earlier count of small units.
Say aloud why the number is different even though the book has not changed.
Discuss: can both counts be right at the same time — for example '5 big cubes' and '12 small cubes' for the same book? Explain how.
Place one large unit on one pan and add small units on the other until it balances, or is as close as possible — count about how many small units equal one large unit.
Answer: if you used really tiny units instead, would the number be bigger or smaller? Why?
activities.intendedInsight: A larger unit means fewer units are needed to balance the same object; the count changes because the unit changed, not because the mass changed. Conversely, smaller units give a larger count.

activities.title: Read the dial by valuing the intervals
feedback: If the child counts the lines/marks to get the number, show that the value lives in the spaces between marks: count intervals, not lines.
If the child is stuck when the pointer is between marks, read to the nearest graduation and name the interval value first.
Prompt to check: how did you decide one interval is worth 100 g? Look at the labelled numbers on the scale.
activities.rationale: Scale-reading errors from counting marks instead of valuing intervals are structurally the same slip as misreading a ruler; establishing interval value first prevents it.
sourceClaims: NCETM mastery tasks assess mass via balance equivalence ('this box weighs 10 kg, how much does each tin weigh?') and via reading dial/kitchen scales to compare masses ('what is the mass of two red bags? which is heavier, red or green? explain'); the Year 1 Big Idea introduces equivalence ('how many cubes are equivalent to the mass of the teddy?').
learnerActions: Look at a dial or kitchen scale marked at regular intervals (e.g. a mark every 100 g).
First work out what ONE interval is worth, e.g. the gap between two marks is 100 g.
Count the intervals (the spaces) from zero up to the pointer, not the marks, to find the mass — e.g. three intervals of 100 g means 300 g.
Read to the nearest graduation when the pointer falls between two marks.
Explain how you knew each mark meant 100 g and not 1 g.
activities.intendedInsight: A graduated scale is read like a number line: establish the value of one interval, then count intervals to the pointer — this is the same skill as reading a ruler.

activities.title: Compare and order masses from readings
feedback: If the child tries to compare counts taken with different-sized units, remind them comparisons only work when the units match.
If ordering is reversed, line up the recorded numbers and check which is larger, then match the symbol.
Encourage a spoken reason for each comparison, not just the symbol.
activities.rationale: Comparing and ordering with >, <, = is an explicit curriculum expectation and consolidates quantification into relational reasoning.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils choose and use appropriate standard units to estimate and measure mass (kg/g) to the nearest appropriate unit using scales, and compare/order mass recording with >, <, =.
learnerActions: Weigh or read several objects and record each mass with its unit.
Decide which is heavier and which is lighter, and put the objects in order by mass.
Record comparisons using the symbols >, < and = (e.g. 300 g > 200 g).
Explain a comparison aloud, e.g. 'the red bag is heavier because 300 g is more than 200 g'.
activities.intendedInsight: Once masses are quantified in the same unit, objects can be compared and ordered numerically and recorded with comparison symbols.

constraints: Units must be identical when counting; mixing unit sizes breaks the count and must be caught before reading.

reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source row asserted that a 3D balance 'adds nothing' over a 2D one and that 'dialogue cannot supply' the practice. These are catalog-preference claims not established by the cited sources; they have been removed. A physical (tactile) balance and a screen model offer different experiences, and discussion can support reasoning about why the count changes — only the measure-and-read practice specifically needs an actual balance and scale.

The inverse relationship (larger unit → fewer units) and the marks-vs-intervals reading principle are supported by the cited progression and curriculum documents at the level of general principle, not as evidence that these specific tasks were tested.

Note on terminology: the topic title pairs 'mass' and 'weight'. For these age 5–6 activities the quantity measured and balanced is mass; 'weight' is used colloquially as children often say it. No change was made to the pedagogy/assessment fields.

The Year 2 standard-units/comparison claim was removed from the non-standard cube-balancing activity and from the dial-reading activity because it supports standard-unit choice, estimation and symbol comparison (activity 4), not those activities' specific equivalence and interval-valuing principles; the NCETM dial/scale-reading claim is retained on the reading activity as support for the convention of reading graduated scales.

(2) Explains bigger cubes are heavier, so FEWER of them balance the same book — the count changed because the unit changed, not the book. (3) Values each interval (100 g) and counts intervals to the pointer, e.g. 300 g, rather than counting marks.

pedagogy.summary: Children measure two or three objects in standard units and then compare and order the results, recording with >, <, and =. The measurement-specific demand on top of number comparison is that a measurement is a number WITH a unit: 1 m is longer than 50 cm even though 1 < 50, so the numbers can only be compared once they are in the same unit (or represented on a common scale).
bestPractices: Measure first, then compare — the comparison is of the measured amounts, not of how the objects look.
Insist the unit travels with the number; make same-unit comparisons before ever mixing units.
Confront the bare-number trap deliberately (1 m vs 50 cm; 300 g vs 1 kg) so children see the number alone can mislead.
Connect >, <, = to the number-comparison children already do, reading the statement aloud ('45 centimetres is greater than 32 centimetres').
Order three measures by repeatedly picking the largest (or smallest), and use = only when the measures are genuinely equal.
keyRepresentations: Two measured bars/ribbons side by side with the symbol between them (45 cm > 32 cm)
A common-scale bar chart that lets 1 m and 50 cm be compared visually
An ordering strip: three containers arranged by measured capacity
The >, <, = symbols read as 'greater than / less than / equal to'
commonMisconceptions: Compares the bare numbers and ignores the units — '50 cm > 1 m because 50 is bigger than 1', or '300 g > 1 kg'.
Reverses the symbol — writes 32 > 45, pointing the 'mouth' the wrong way.
Orders by appearance rather than by the measured amounts.
Uses = loosely for measures that are merely close, not equal.

learn.summary: Children measure two or three objects in standard units, then compare and order the measured amounts and record using >, <, and =. Measure first, keep the unit travelling with the number, confront the bare-number trap deliberately, and use = only for genuinely equal measures.

activities.title: Measure, then place the symbol
feedback: If a learner writes 50 cm > 1 m because '50 is bigger', have them line both up on one shared ruler or convert to the same unit (1 m = 100 cm) so the metre visibly towers over the 50 cm; then re-record the true statement 1 m > 50 cm.
If the symbol is reversed (e.g. 32 > 45), re-anchor 'the open side faces the bigger amount' and have them read the statement aloud to check it matches what they mean.
When correct, confirm by reading the full statement aloud with the unit included, e.g. '45 centimetres is greater than 32 centimetres'.
activities.rationale: Measuring before comparing ties the symbol to a measured amount rather than appearance, and a deliberate unit-mismatch pair surfaces the bare-number trap so the 'keep the unit' idea is experienced, not just stated. An optional interactive version may let a child drag the symbol between two readings for immediate feedback and slide a mismatched pair onto one common ruler so the true sizes show.
sourceClaims: In measurement the concept of unit is crucial and unit size is critical: counting discrete items often convinces students that the size of what is counted does not matter, but for measurement the unit must always be considered — a number is meaningful only with its unit ('what are you counting?' -> 'centimeters'). The larger the unit, the fewer units in a given measurement (inverse relationship).
Year 2 pupils compare and order lengths, mass, volume/capacity and record the results using >, <, and =; this parallels comparing and ordering two-digit numbers with the same symbols.
learnerActions: Measure two objects in the same unit and write each measurement with its unit (e.g. a pencil case at 32 cm and a book at 45 cm).
Place >, <, or = between the two readings so the statement is true, then read it aloud ('45 centimetres is greater than 32 centimetres').
Check the symbol points its open side toward the larger amount.

Repeat with a mixed-unit pair, such as a 1 m ribbon and a 50 cm ribbon: before deciding, bring both to the same unit or line them up on one common ruler/scale, then record the true comparison (1 m > 50 cm).
activities.intendedInsight: A measurement is a number together with its unit; you must compare the actual amounts, not the bare digits. When units differ, convert to a shared unit first: 1 m equals 100 cm, which is more than 50 cm, so 1 m > 50 cm even though 1 is a smaller number than 50.

activities.title: Order three measured things
feedback: If a learner orders by how things look, require the measured value to be written beside each object first, then re-order using only those numbers; discuss the case where looks and measures disagree.
If = is used for measures that are only close, ask them to compare the exact readings and decide whether they are truly equal or whether > or < is correct.
When units differ across the three items, prompt converting to a shared unit or placing them on one common scale before ordering.
activities.rationale: Writing the measured value beside each object forces attention onto the numbers, and a looks-vs-measures conflict case makes the measure-not-appearance point concrete. Three-way ordering extends two-way comparison and gives a natural place to discuss when = truly applies.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils compare and order lengths, mass, volume/capacity and record the results using >, <, and =; this parallels comparing and ordering two-digit numbers with the same symbols.
learnerActions: Measure three objects (e.g. three containers for capacity) and write the measured value, with its unit, next to each.
Arrange them from least to most by repeatedly picking the smallest remaining measured amount (or from most to least by repeatedly picking the largest remaining measured amount).
Include a case where how big the objects look disagrees with what they measure, and order by the measurements anyway.
Use = only between two measures that are genuinely equal, not merely close.
activities.intendedInsight: Ordering is done on the measured amounts, not on appearance, and = is reserved for truly equal measures.

activities.title: Reference card for the symbols
feedback: Prompt the learner to read each statement aloud with units, confirming the words match the symbol.
Follow a reference check with an actual measure-and-compare task, since reading a fixed example does not by itself show whether the learner can choose and place the symbol for a new pair.

Reviewing a fixed example checks recognition of the notation but does not itself elicit independent production of a comparison.
learnerActions: Study a labelled example such as '45 cm > 32 cm' and say what >, <, and = mean ('greater than', 'less than', 'equal to').
Describe why the open side of the symbol faces the larger amount.
Explain in words why a mixed-unit statement like '1 m > 50 cm' is true even though 1 is smaller than 50 (because 1 m is 100 cm).
activities.intendedInsight: Secures the meaning and reading of the >, <, = notation as support for making one's own comparisons.

Include at least one deliberate mixed-unit pair (e.g. 1 m vs 50 cm, 300 g vs 1 kg) where the bare-number guess is wrong, so the misconception is confronted and resolved by converting to a shared unit or using a common scale.

Explain mixed-unit comparisons by converting to a shared unit, not by a 'bigger unit wins' shortcut, which does not hold in general (e.g. 500 cm > 1 m).

The original recommendation framed the insight as '1 beats 50 because the unit behind the number is bigger'; this heuristic is not generally valid (a larger unit does not always yield a larger measurement), so the insight was reworded to compare amounts via conversion to a shared unit.

responseLevels.gap: Compares by the bare numbers (50 cm > 1 m), reverses the symbol, or orders by appearance without measuring.

Say: 'Measure these, then write which is bigger using the >, <, or = sign, and put these three containers in order from least to most.' Watch whether they attend to the units, which way the symbol points, and whether they order by measuring or by looks.
