topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Measuring length
topic.description: Order three objects by length and compare the lengths of two objects indirectly using a third object
evidence: Put three ribbons in order from shortest to longest
Use a piece of string to compare the heights of two objects that cannot be placed side by side
Explain that if A is longer than B and B is longer than C, then A is longer than C
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has three pencils of different lengths but can only compare two at a time, can they figure out which is longest — by using a third pencil as a go-between?

pedagogy.summary: Children learn to seriate three or more objects by length and to compare two objects that cannot be placed side by side by using a third object (a string or strip) as an intermediary. The reasoning underneath is transitivity: if A is longer than B and B is longer than C, then A is longer than C — and a portable copy of one length lets you carry a comparison across a gap.
bestPractices: Serial ordering: give three (then more) ribbons or cube-towers and encourage a strategy — pick the shortest, then the next shortest — rather than random trial-and-error.
Set a genuine problem where two objects cannot be moved together (a doorway vs a bookshelf) so the child discovers a string/strip as a portable copy of a length.
Voice the transitive inference explicitly: 'the door is taller than the string; the shelf is shorter than the string; so the door is taller than the shelf.'
Keep the intermediary constant — uncut, unstretched, aligned at the same end — because a re-cut or stretched string breaks the comparison; use it to build conservation of length.
Use insert-into-series tasks: 'where does this new ribbon go?' to push beyond trial-and-error toward a mental image of an increasing series.
keyRepresentations: A set of three-plus ribbons or cube-towers arranged as an increasing 'staircase'
A length of string or paper strip used as an intermediary copy of a length
The seriation staircase image (each step the smallest increase in length)
commonMisconceptions: Compares only pairs and never chains the inference — insists on placing A directly against C instead of reasoning through the intermediary.
Orders by trial-and-error with no image of an increasing series, and cannot say where a new object should be inserted.
Does not keep the intermediary constant — stretches, re-cuts, or re-aligns the string between the two comparisons.
Non-conservation: believes the string's length changed when it was bent or moved.

learn.summary: Children learn to seriate three or more objects by length and to compare two objects that cannot be placed side by side by using a third object (string or paper strip) as a fixed intermediary length. The underlying reasoning is transitivity: if A is longer than B and B is longer than C, then A is longer than C — and a string kept at one fixed length lets a comparison be carried across a gap. Enactive ordering and carrying an intermediary build the reasoning; recognition formats and static displays can check or summarise it.

activities.title: Carrying a length across a gap with a string
feedback: If the child says the objects 'can't be compared, they're too far apart' or tries to move one object to the other: model comparing the string to A, then to B, and voice 'A vs string, string vs B, so A vs B'; secure direct side-by-side comparison first so the string has a length to stand for.

If the child re-cuts, stretches, or re-aligns the string between the two comparisons: emphasise the string must stay the same single length for both objects; mark its end and align the same starting point each time. (Setting the string to match one object's length at the start is fine — the rule is only that it must not change between comparisons.)

If the child says the string 'got shorter/longer' after it is bent or moved: treat this as a conservation stage, not carelessness — straighten-and-compare so the child sees the length is unchanged, and revisit later rather than correcting hard.

Probe: 'How do you know this one is taller if you never put them next to each other?' and 'If the string were longer than BOTH objects, could you still tell which is taller? How?' (This last case shows the need to compare how each object lines up against the string, not just a longer/shorter label.)
activities.rationale: Indirect comparison via a third object is a Grade 1/Year 2 measurement expectation, with the canonical task of judging which of two paths or objects is longer by laying one length of string along each (one longer than the string, the other shorter). Enacting the carry makes the transitive inference concrete; keeping the intermediary at one fixed length between comparisons develops conservation of length.
sourceClaims: The Transitivity Principle — if A is longer than B and B is longer than C then A is longer than C — is a Grade 1 expectation used for indirect comparison when direct comparison is impossible; the canonical example is judging which of two paths is longer via a length of string laid along each (one path longer than the string, the other shorter).

The Length Indirect Comparer compares two objects by representing them with a third object (e.g. a piece of string) and discussion focuses on transitive inference; a child at this level may use a ruler but often ignores the starting point. Serial Orderer levels: children first order 3–5 lengths by trial-and-error, then build a mental image of an increasing series and seriate by choosing the shortest then the 'smallest difference' next, and learn to insert a length by making it longer than those on one side and shorter than those on the other.
Year 2 pupils compare and order lengths and heights and use indirect comparison / a third object to compare objects that cannot be placed together.
learnerActions: Face two objects (e.g. two cube-towers, or a tall object by the door and a shelf across the room) that are clearly too far apart to bring together and line up.

Hold a fixed length of string against the first object, aligned at the same starting end, and note whether that object is taller or shorter than the string; keep the string's length unchanged for both comparisons (do not change it between the two objects).
Keeping the string uncut and unstretched, carry it across to the second object and see whether it overshoots the top or falls short.

Compare each object to the same string and state the conclusion, voicing the transitive chain — e.g. 'this one is taller than the string; that one is shorter than the string; so this one is taller than that one.'
Try a second far-apart pair to transfer the idea.

Optional screen version: drag a fixed length of string to one tower, then carry it to the other and watch whether it overshoots or falls short, so the transitive step is something the child performs rather than is told.
activities.intendedInsight: A string kept at one fixed length can be carried to a place where two objects cannot meet, letting you decide which is longer by comparing each to the same intermediary.

activities.title: Building and extending a seriation staircase
feedback: If the child reorders only by trial and error, succeeds by luck, and cannot place a fourth ribbon: do not drill formal ordering rules or push insertion logic prematurely; give more compare-two experience and 'pick the shortest each time' prompts — a mental image of the series consolidates with age and working memory.
Probe: 'Where would a new, in-between ribbon go in your line? How did you decide?'
Confirm success when the child seriates by smallest-difference and can reliably insert new items.
activities.rationale: Serial ordering develops from trial-and-error toward a mental image of an increasing series; a shortest-first (then smallest-difference) strategy and insert-into-series tasks push beyond lucky guessing, and insertion logic draws on the same longer-than/shorter-than reasoning as transitivity.
sourceClaims: The Length Indirect Comparer compares two objects by representing them with a third object (e.g. a piece of string) and discussion focuses on transitive inference; a child at this level may use a ruler but often ignores the starting point. Serial Orderer levels: children first order 3–5 lengths by trial-and-error, then build a mental image of an increasing series and seriate by choosing the shortest then the 'smallest difference' next, and learn to insert a length by making it longer than those on one side and shorter than those on the other.
Year 2 pupils compare and order lengths and heights and use indirect comparison / a third object to compare objects that cannot be placed together.
learnerActions: Order three ribbons or cube-towers from shortest to longest using a strategy — pick the shortest, then the next shortest — rather than random swapping.
Progress to ordering five or more into an increasing 'staircase' where each step is the smallest available increase in length.
Check the finished line and fix any inversion (a shorter item placed after a longer one).

Take a new ribbon and decide where it belongs: it goes after every shorter ribbon and before every longer one, so it may land in between two ribbons or at either end if it is the shortest or longest of all.
Optional screen version: drag a fourth ribbon into a staircase that only settles when it sits above the shorter and below the longer neighbour, with a nudge when an inversion is left.
activities.intendedInsight: Transitivity becomes the rule that orders a whole set: when no two lengths are equal, each item is longer than everything before it and shorter than everything after, so a new item of a different length from all the others slots into exactly one place (if it matches an existing length, it can go right next to that item).

activities.title: Naming the transitive chain (check and consolidate)
feedback: Confirm a correct ordering and a correct spoken/selected answer; where the child answers the inference but cannot show it with objects, return to the string-carrying activity.
Use the staircase display only to summarise, then ask the child to re-derive the chain with real ribbons or string.
activities.rationale: An ordering step and a multiple-choice inference question match the ordering and transitivity evidence and are useful for checking understanding; a tap-to-reveal staircase can display and name the chain. These formats verify and consolidate but, on their own, elicit recognition rather than independent construction of the comparison.
sourceClaims: The Transitivity Principle — if A is longer than B and B is longer than C then A is longer than C — is a Grade 1 expectation used for indirect comparison when direct comparison is impossible; the canonical example is judging which of two paths is longer via a length of string laid along each (one path longer than the string, the other shorter).
learnerActions: Order a given set of ribbons shortest to longest as an ordering check.
Answer a transitive-inference question in words, e.g. 'The bookshelf is shorter than the string and the door is taller than the string — which is taller?'
Review a staircase display of the 'A > B > C, so A > C' chain, naming each term, as a summary reference after doing the hands-on work.
activities.intendedInsight: The transitive conclusion can be stated and recognised in words once it has been built through ordering and carrying an intermediary.

constraints: The learning objective is enactive: children must actually order objects and carry a constant intermediary, not only recognise or restate the rule. Recognition-only formats (choosing the taller from a worded prompt, tapping to reveal a chain) check or consolidate but do not elicit independent construction of the comparison.

A static staircase display can summarise and name the 'A>B>C so A>C' chain but does not let the child perform the ordering or the string comparison that carries the concept; use it as a reference, not the main activity.

The intermediary must be kept the SAME length throughout both comparisons — uncut, unstretched, aligned at the same starting end — or the comparison is invalid; this requirement is itself part of building conservation of length. Either approach is acceptable: a single fixed independent string compared to both objects, or a string set to one object's length then carried unchanged to the other; what is invalid is changing the string's length between the two comparisons.

Length comparison here is one-dimensional, so a flat staircase and a string are sufficient; a 3D spatial environment is not required for this objective (a scope note, not a claim that 3D can never aid any measurement learning).
Non-conservation of the intermediary and trial-and-error seriation are developmental stages, not errors to drill away; provide more experience rather than hard correction.

assess.correctAnswer: For the three ribbons, the child builds a correct series — selecting shortest then next-shortest, or checking and fixing inversions. For the two far-apart objects, the child uses the string as an intermediary: matches it to one object, keeps it uncut and aligned at the same end, carries it to the other, and states the conclusion — ideally voicing the transitive link ('this one is taller than the string, that one is shorter than it, so this one is taller').

errorPatterns.pattern: No transitive inference — pairwise only: sees the two far-apart objects as simply not comparable, or insists on carrying one object to the other, never using the string as a proxy for a length.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model matching the string to A, then to B, and voice the chain 'A vs string, string vs B, so A vs B'; secure direct comparison first so the intermediary has something to stand for.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the objects 'can't be compared, they're too far apart', or tries to move one object across; ignores the string as a stand-in.

errorPatterns.pattern: Trial-and-error seriation with no series image: orders three by random swapping, succeeds by luck, and cannot say where a new ribbon would be inserted.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill formal ordering rules or push insertion logic prematurely; give more compare-two experience and 'pick the shortest each time' prompts — a mental image of the series consolidates with working memory and age.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reorders by trial and error, no shortest-first strategy; stuck when asked to insert a fourth ribbon.

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not keep the intermediary constant: re-cuts, stretches, or re-aligns the string between the two comparisons, so it no longer copies one fixed length.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Emphasise the string is a fixed copy of exactly one length; mark its end and align the same starting point for both objects before comparing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: String is stretched taut for one object and slack for the other, cut shorter, or measured from a different end each time.

errorPatterns.pattern: Non-conservation of the intermediary: believes the string's length changed when it was bent or moved.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT treat as carelessness — it is a conservation stage; straighten-and-compare so the child sees the length is preserved, and revisit later rather than correcting hard.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: After the string is curved or repositioned, the child says 'it got shorter/longer' and re-judges.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot compare the far-apart pair (calls it impossible or tries to carry an object), or orders the three only by random trial with no reasoning offered.

responseLevels.partial: Uses the string for one comparison OR orders the three correctly, but treats these as separate tricks — cannot articulate the transitive link, or orders three yet cannot reliably insert a fourth or transfer the string idea to a new far-apart pair.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give three ribbons of clearly different lengths and say 'Put these in order, shortest to longest.' Ordering by shortest-first versus random swapping separates a mental image of an increasing series from lucky guessing.

topic.name: Measuring length (age 6+)
topic.description: Measure the length of an object using same-size length units laid end to end with no gaps or overlaps
evidence: Measure a book by laying paper clips end to end and counting them
Understand that the length measurement is the number of units that span the object
Avoid gaps and overlaps when placing units
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is measuring the length of a table using identical toy bricks, can they lay them end to end with no gaps — and tell you how many bricks long the table is?

pedagogy.summary: Measuring length with units means covering the object from end to end with same-size units laid with no gaps or overlaps, and reporting the COUNT of those units as the length (CCSS Progression). Two ideas must come together: the units must be identical in size, and they must tile the whole span (endpoint to endpoint) without gaps or overlaps. The classic obstacle is that children treat the task as 'put some objects along it and count them' — counting discrete objects rather than measuring a continuous length — so they leave gaps, mix unit sizes, or start partway along, and still confidently read off a number. Inhelder, Sinclair and Bovet's matches task captures it: children called a row of 6 short matches 'longer' than 5 long ones because it had more units.
bestPractices: Insist units are laid flush end to end, filling the object from one endpoint to the other with no gaps and no overlaps — make full coverage the rule, not decoration
Use a mixed-up puppet who leaves gaps, overlaps units, or starts in the middle, so children diagnose and fix the error (self-checking beats being told)

Confront the same-size-unit principle directly: measure one object with big clips and again with small clips, or run the matches demonstration, so 'more units' is seen NOT to mean 'longer' unless the units match
Emphasise starting flush at one end and that the length is the number of units that SPAN the object, not just the units you happened to place
Ask 'what are you counting?' — the answer is length-units — and count the units (spaces), not the marks or junctions where units meet
Bridge to rulers later by having children build a unit ruler from copies of one unit, so the ruler is understood as iterated units rather than a strip of numerals
keyRepresentations: A book with same-size paper clips laid end to end along it, flush at the start, no gaps
A mixed-up puppet's row with visible gaps/overlaps for the child to correct
Two rows of equal total length — few long units vs many short units — to break 'more units = longer' (the matches task)
A home-made unit ruler built by iterating copies of a single unit
commonMisconceptions: Leaving gaps or overlaps between units but still counting them and reporting a length
Using different-sized units and treating the counts as comparable — concluding the object with MORE units is longer regardless of unit size
Not spanning the whole object — starting the first unit inset from the edge, or stopping before the far end, then counting
Counting the marks/junctions or endpoints rather than the units themselves, producing an off-by-one length

learn.summary: Teaches length measurement as tiling an object end to end with identical units laid flush, no gaps or overlaps, and reporting the COUNT of those units as the length. Two load-bearing ideas must hold together: units are the same size, and they fill the whole span from one endpoint to the other. The core obstacle is treating measurement as 'put some objects down and count them' — so children leave gaps, mix unit sizes, or start partway along and still confidently read off a number. The Inhelder/Sinclair/Bovet matches task captures it: children called a row of 6 short matches 'longer' than 5 long ones because it had more units.

activities.title: Measure a book with paper clips, filling the whole span
feedback: If gaps are left, highlight the uncovered stretch: 'this bit wasn't measured — the clips don't cover all of the book yet'

If the first clip starts inset from the edge or the last stretch is left uncovered, prompt: 'start right at one end and keep going to the other end — the length is the number of clips that SPAN the book'; if the leftover bit is shorter than one clip, agree it is 'about' or 'a bit more than' that many clips
When the span is fully tiled flush with no gaps or overlaps, confirm the count is now an honest length: the number of clips that cover the book end to end
For the home-made ruler, point out that each mark is just where one unit ends and the next begins
activities.rationale: Gaps, overlaps and short spanning are errors of action; letting the child lay and adjust real units and check coverage with a finger makes 'fill the whole length' a rule they enforce rather than are told. An optional interactive version can make gaps glow and withhold a settled count until the span is fully covered, so the consequence of a gap is felt immediately. Building a ruler from iterated copies bridges to standard tools as units-in-a-row.
sourceClaims: Measuring length is choosing a unit and iterating it end to end alongside the object; the length is the number of units required to go from one end to the other WITHOUT gaps or overlaps, using SAME-SIZE units. In the Inhelder/Sinclair/Bovet matches task, children called a row of 6 shorter matches longer than a row of 5 longer matches because it had more units — counting units while ignoring that the units differed in size; first graders can learn that units must be the same size. Students should count the length-units, not the end-points, and learn that '1' on a ruler represents the space to the first mark, not the mark itself.

At the End-to-End Length Measurer level a child lays units end to end to measure an object but may not recognise the need for equal-length units; activities challenge children to fill lengths from endpoint to endpoint without gaps or overlaps, and because children are often not concerned with accuracy the best activities are self-checking (e.g. a mixed-up puppet who makes gap/overlap mistakes for children to correct).

KS1 pupils should measure and begin to record lengths/heights and choose and use appropriate standard units to measure length to the nearest appropriate unit using rulers, developing from measuring with units laid along an object.
learnerActions: Lay identical paper clips along a book, starting flush at one end, so they continue end to end to the far end with no gaps and no overlaps
Run a finger along the book from the very start to the very end to check that the clips cover ALL of it

Report the length as the number of clips that span the book; if the last clip sticks out past the end or a small bit is left that is shorter than a clip, say 'about' or 'a bit more than' that many clips
Repair a row that someone else laid with obvious gaps or overlaps, nudging the clips flush until the whole span is tiled
Build a small ruler by snapping copies of a single clip into a row, to see that a ruler is just units lined up
activities.intendedInsight: A length is the number of equal units that completely fill an object from end to end; gaps, overlaps, or a row that starts inset mean the count does not yet report the true length.

activities.title: Fix the mixed-up puppet's measurement
feedback: If the child accepts a gappy row's count, point to the gap: 'is every bit of the pencil covered? the clips skip this part, so the count isn't the whole length'
Praise diagnosing the specific error ('there's a gap here', 'these overlap', 'it starts too late') over simply restating a number
After repair, have the child re-run the finger-sweep to confirm full coverage
activities.rationale: Self-checking against a deliberately wrong model is better than being told the rule, because children are often untroubled by inaccuracy; diagnosing another's error externalises the principle and makes the child the checker. A puppet or a pre-laid row the child must judge both serve this.
sourceClaims: At the End-to-End Length Measurer level a child lays units end to end to measure an object but may not recognise the need for equal-length units; activities challenge children to fill lengths from endpoint to endpoint without gaps or overlaps, and because children are often not concerned with accuracy the best activities are self-checking (e.g. a mixed-up puppet who makes gap/overlap mistakes for children to correct).
learnerActions: Look at a row laid by a 'mixed-up' puppet that has visible gaps, overlapping units, or units that start in the middle
Explain what the puppet did wrong
Re-lay the units correctly so they fill the span flush, end to end, with no gaps or overlaps, and give the corrected length
Judge a stated count (e.g. 'I measured this pencil and got 6') against a row that has an obvious gap, and say whether the number is right
activities.intendedInsight: A count is only a length when the units completely tile the span; spotting and fixing gaps/overlaps is the child's job, not something to accept on trust.

activities.title: Does 'more units' mean 'longer'? The mixed-size challenge
feedback: If the child says the object with more (smaller) units is longer, lay the two measurements side by side so the equal spans are visible: the object didn't change, only the size of the unit did
If the child mixes big and small clips, ask them to lay one measurement in equal units and compare: 'which count can we trust, and why?'
Confirm the key idea when stated: counts can only be compared when the units are the same size
activities.rationale: Directly confronting the same-size-unit principle by measuring one object with two unit sizes, and by building the wrong mixed count then contrasting it with an equal-unit measure, targets the exact misconception that 'more units = longer'. The matches task is a classic research demonstration of this error.
sourceClaims: Measuring length is choosing a unit and iterating it end to end alongside the object; the length is the number of units required to go from one end to the other WITHOUT gaps or overlaps, using SAME-SIZE units. In the Inhelder/Sinclair/Bovet matches task, children called a row of 6 shorter matches longer than a row of 5 longer matches because it had more units — counting units while ignoring that the units differed in size; first graders can learn that units must be the same size. Students should count the length-units, not the end-points, and learn that '1' on a ruler represents the space to the first mark, not the mark itself.
learnerActions: Measure one object with large clips, then measure the SAME object again with small clips, and compare the two counts
Measure a second object with a jumbled mix of big and small clips, then lay equal-size clips beside it
Answer: 'I measured this ribbon with big clips and got 4, and with little clips I got 8 — did the ribbon get longer? Why did the numbers change?'
Answer: 'Could I measure this with a mix of big and little clips? Why not?'
Optionally run the matches version: compare a row of a few long matches with a row of many short matches that cover the same distance
activities.intendedInsight: More units does NOT mean longer when the units are different sizes; the same object gives a bigger count with smaller units without getting any longer, and mixing unit sizes within one measurement makes the count fail to report a length because each unit covers a different amount.

activities.title: Count the units, not the joins
feedback: If the child counts the points where clips meet (or the clip ends), ask 'what are you counting — the clips, or the joins between them?' and have them touch each clip once
Treat this as a counting slip to tighten, not a conceptual gap — the child who makes it still understands coverage and equal units
Link forward: on a ruler, the number 1 is written at the end of the first unit; it tells us one whole unit has been covered from the 0 end, so we count the spaces covered, not the tick marks
activities.rationale: Distinguishing units from junctions prevents a common off-by-one error and lays groundwork for reading a ruler, where the number at each tick mark tells how many whole units lie between 0 and that mark, so counting tick marks (including 0) gives one too many. This is a precision/counting refinement rather than a reteach of the core concept.
sourceClaims: Measuring length is choosing a unit and iterating it end to end alongside the object; the length is the number of units required to go from one end to the other WITHOUT gaps or overlaps, using SAME-SIZE units. In the Inhelder/Sinclair/Bovet matches task, children called a row of 6 shorter matches longer than a row of 5 longer matches because it had more units — counting units while ignoring that the units differed in size; first graders can learn that units must be the same size. Students should count the length-units, not the end-points, and learn that '1' on a ruler represents the space to the first mark, not the mark itself.
learnerActions: After laying clips along an object, state the count and then point to each thing being counted
Count the units (the clips/spaces), touching each one once, rather than the points where units meet or the end marks
Check a row where the count might be off by one: 'you counted 7 — point to each thing you counted'
activities.intendedInsight: The length is the number of units (the spaces covered), not the number of marks or junctions where units meet; counting the joins gives an off-by-one answer.

activities.title: Pick the correct measurement (recognition check)
feedback: For a chosen gappy or overlapping row, prompt the child to explain whether the whole object is covered
For a mixed-unit distractor, ask whether the units are all the same size and why that matters

If the child says the row with more short units is longer, align the two rows end to end to show the spans match — the object is the same length; only the unit size differs, so the bigger count does not tell us which is longer
When the valid row is chosen, have the child state the two reasons it is valid: equal units AND full end-to-end coverage
activities.rationale: Choosing among correct and flawed rows and counting spanning units checks the concept efficiently. This recognition format confirms whether a child can judge a measurement but does not by itself show they can lay and adjust units independently, so pair it with the hands-on tasks above.
learnerActions: From several rows laid along an object, choose the one that measures it correctly, where distractors have gaps, overlaps, or mixed-size units
Count the units spanning an object and give the number
Compare two rows that cover the SAME span — a few long units versus many short units — and judge whether the row with more (shorter) units is actually longer, explaining your reasoning
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising a valid measurement means checking for full coverage, no gaps/overlaps, and equal units; and when two rows cover the same span, a bigger count made of smaller units does not mean the object is longer.

constraints: This skill is for roughly ages 6–7 (KS1 / first grade); the goal is non-standard units laid end to end, bridging toward rulers later, not yet fluent ruler reading.

The central evidence is the child actually laying units and counting; recognition-only tasks (choosing the correct row) confirm judgement but do not elicit the independent construction and adjustment of a tiled measurement, so they are a check, not a substitute.

A labelled static picture can show why a gappy or mixed row is wrong on tap, but it cannot let the child lay and adjust units; the corrective action stays demonstrated rather than practised, so use it only as a supporting scaffold.

An interactive drag-to-tile tool that flags gaps/overlaps and withholds a settled count is one effective way to make the consequence of a gap immediate; the same learning is achievable with real clips and a finger-sweep check. These are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not a required medium.
Measuring units along an object is a planar task; a 3D handling environment is not needed and adds handling cost without sharpening the gaps/overlaps/equal-unit ideas.
Keep real materials (paper clips, matches, ribbon, books) and physical or screen tiling as approximations of the same idea; neither is universally necessary.

When comparing lengths by their counts, hold the unit size fixed: a bigger count with the same-size unit means longer, but a bigger count made of smaller units on the same span does not. The counts as numbers can still be compared (8 is more than 4); they just do not show which length is longer unless the units are the same size.

One source (UK National Curriculum KS1) was marked verified:false in the original row; treat its claim as unconfirmed even where it is cited to support the bridge toward rulers.

Original diagnostic guidance warns against demonstrating before setting tasks when assessing; teaching activities here deliberately include modelling and feedback — keep assessment separate from instruction so a 'watch first' diagnostic remains valid.

The original artefact notes asserted that a static image 'cannot' let the child practise and that a conversation 'cannot render' the measurement; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal claims about what a medium can teach.

The recognition activity's few-long-vs-many-short comparison is framed so that both equal-span rows are valid measures with their own same-size units; the item asks whether more units means longer (it does not), not which single row is 'valid'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set tasks and WATCH — do not demonstrate first. (1) Give the child a book and a pile of identical paper clips: 'Measure how long the book is.' pedagogy.summary: Children move from 'which is longer?' to 'how much longer?' — measuring both objects in the same standard unit and subtracting the smaller from the larger to give the difference expressed with its unit ('7 cm longer'). This is the additive-comparison (difference-unknown) structure applied to measured lengths, and it is best made visible as the overhang between two bars aligned at a common baseline.
bestPractices: Measure both objects in the same unit first, then find the difference by subtracting the smaller from the larger.
Demand the amount, not just the direction: the answer is '7 cm taller', not 'the shelf is taller'.
Make the difference visible — align the two lengths at a common baseline (bar model / number line) so the overhang IS the difference.
Use comparison ('difference unknown') word problems and represent them with tape/bar diagrams and an equation with the unknown.
Keep both measures in one unit before subtracting; expose the error of subtracting across different units.
keyRepresentations: Two bars aligned at a common baseline with the overhang marked as the difference
A number line showing both lengths from 0 and the gap between their endpoints

Treats the difference as the sum, or adds when the problem asks how much longer.

topic.name: Estimating Lengths
topic.description: Estimate lengths using units of inches, feet, centimetres, and metres
evidence: Estimate the length of a classroom object before measuring it

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a car parked outside, can they estimate roughly how many metres long it is — and then check whether their guess was reasonable?

pedagogy.summary: Children learn to estimate lengths in standard units by building a 'mental ruler' — anchoring a guess to a known referent (a fingernail ≈ 1 cm, a big stride ≈ 1 m, a doorway height ≈ 2 m) and iterating that image — then measuring to check and revise. Require a committed estimate BEFORE measuring, so estimation is a real prediction, not a post-hoc guess.
Model the mental-ruler strategy: iterate the image of a unit along the object, or compare it to a known length.
Always follow up by measuring and evaluating closeness ('were you over or under? by how much?') to recalibrate the mental ruler.
Choose the appropriate unit for the scale being estimated (cm for a book, m for the playground).

learn.summary: Children estimate lengths in standard units (inches, feet, centimetres and metres) by building a 'mental ruler' — anchoring a guess to a known referent (a fingernail ≈ 1 cm, a US quarter ≈ 1 inch across, a 12-inch ruler = 1 foot, a metre stick = 1 m, a doorway ≈ 2 m tall) and mentally iterating that image along an object — then measuring to check and revise. The core cycle is: commit an estimate BEFORE measuring, measure, then judge how close ('over or under? by how much?') and adjust the next estimate. Estimation follows hands-on measuring, and research-informed practice favours explicit strategy (benchmarks, mental iteration) over unstructured guessing. The unit and benchmark must fit the scale (cm or inches for a book, m or feet for a playground).

activities.title: Estimate–measure–revise with a benchmark referent
feedback: If a number is given with no basis ('a hundred?') and is wildly off, prompt: 'What could you compare it to? Your fingernail is about 1 cm — how many of those fit along the book?'
If the number is sensible but the unit is wrong-sized (a book at '20 m', a pencil at '15 feet'), ask: 'Is a book really as long as 20 metre sticks? What unit matches something this size?'
After measuring, always ask 'Were you over or under? By how much? What will you change next time?' so the estimate and measurement are related, not treated separately.
When the scene jumps to a large distance, prompt switching referent: 'A fingernail won't help here — what about a metre stick, or a foot-long ruler?'
activities.rationale: After experience with measuring, Grade 2 learners estimate lengths; skilled estimators move between measurements and magnitudes on a 'mental ruler', and research suggests explicitly teaching strategies (iterating a mental image of the unit, comparing with a known measurement) and benchmark lengths rather than relying on unstructured guess-and-check. Committing before measuring makes estimation a genuine prediction, and the compare-and-revise step with a recording strip is what improves the mental ruler.

learnerActions: Before measuring, commit an estimate for a given object in an appropriate unit and say how you worked it out (e.g. 'my fingernail is about 1 cm, so this book is around 20 cm').

Measure the object and compare to your estimate: were you over or under, and by how much?
Record each estimate, the measured length and the difference on an estimate–measure–difference strip, so the gap is visible and comparable across objects.
State what you would change for the next estimate, then try the next object and check whether your estimates get closer.
Work across different scales (book → desk → whiteboard → playground) and switch benchmark and unit to match the scale.

Keep a benchmark card beside you as a reference while doing the estimate–measure–revise activity.

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to measure a piece of fabric about 80 cm long, can they pick the right tool — a short ruler or a tape measure — and use it accurately?

pedagogy.summary: Children consolidate the use of standard measuring tools — ruler, metre stick, measuring tape — by choosing the right tool for the object, aligning the zero-point with one end (even when the ruler's 0 is not at its physical edge), and reading the result as an accumulation of unit-lengths in centimetres and metres (and inches and feet). The load-bearing idea is that a numeral on the ruler names the amount of space already covered from zero, not the tick mark itself.
bestPractices: Build the ruler from iterated units first — a child-made paper ruler — so the numerals mean 'units so far' rather than labels on tick marks.
Teach zero-point alignment explicitly, including the 'broken ruler' / offset-zero case where the scale starts at 3 and the length is the difference.
Practise tool selection: match the tool to the object (ruler for a pencil, tape for a table, metre stick for a room) and discuss why.
Stress accumulation of distance: reading '8' names the space covered by 8 units, not the 8th mark or line.
Connect unit size to count (the inverse relationship) when switching between centimetres and inches — smaller units give a larger count for the same length.
keyRepresentations: Centimetre / inch ruler
Metre stick and measuring tape
A 'broken ruler' whose scale starts at 3 (offset zero)
A child-made unit ruler built by iterating one unit

commonMisconceptions: Starts the object at the '1' mark, or reads the last numeral touched — treats numerals as start-signals, not accumulated units.
Cannot cope with an offset or broken ruler; assumes measuring must begin at 0 or the physical edge.
Counts the marks / hash-lines rather than the spaces (unit-lengths) between them, giving a fencepost error of one too many.
Chooses an inappropriate tool — e.g. a short ruler to measure a room by repeated flipping.

learn.summary: Children consolidate measuring length with standard tools (ruler, metre stick, measuring tape) by selecting the right tool for the object, aligning the zero-point with one end — even when the ruler's 0 sits inside the physical edge — and reading the result as an accumulation of unit-lengths (cm/m, inches/feet). The load-bearing idea is that a numeral on the ruler names the amount of space already covered from zero, not the tick mark itself. Key misconceptions targeted: starting at '1', failing with an offset/broken ruler, counting marks instead of spaces (fencepost error), and poor tool choice.

activities.title: Drag-and-align: the chipped-edge ruler
feedback: If the object is aligned at the chipped physical edge, the live readout is wrong — slide the object's end to the actual 0 mark and the reading snaps to the true length (the arbitrary chipped gap is handled by repositioning, not by subtracting a fraction).

If the object's end sits at a whole numeral other than 0 (e.g. the start aligned at '1', or a scale that starts at 3), the length is the end numeral minus the start numeral — not the end numeral read off directly.
For a broken ruler where the object spans from 3 to 12, the length is 12 − 3 = 9 units; prompt: 'this ruler starts at 3 — how long is the object, and how do you know?'
Ask 'does the 8 mean the 8th line, or the space covered up to that mark?' to surface the accumulation idea.
If the same tool is chosen for every object, ask 'which tool fits this length?' — e.g. a short ruler flipped repeatedly across a room accumulates error.

Connect back: when reading a manufactured ruler, the numeral still means 'units of space so far', exactly as on the home-made one.
Note: a paper strip has slight thickness and is a physical approximation; the scale it represents is an idealised line of equal unit-lengths.

activities.title: Broken-ruler and tool-matching diagnostic items

If the child refuses because 'it doesn't start at 0', affirm that the object's start can line up with any whole-numbered mark, not only 0, and the length is the difference between the end and start readings.

constraints: Target ages roughly 7–8; procedural skill of selecting and using rulers, metre sticks and measuring tapes in cm/m and inches/feet.
A fixed annotated ruler is a reference scaffold: it conveys the meaning of numerals but cannot rehearse alignment, repositioning, or live reading; pair it with active measuring.
A broken-ruler/tool-matching check is a discriminating assessment of the skill more than a builder of it; use it alongside hands-on tasks, not instead of them.
Reading or recognising a stated value does not itself elicit the independent act of aligning a tool and reading a length; keep genuine construction/measuring in the core tasks.
Live-recompute readouts, running unit-counts, drag-to-align, and tool-pickers are offered as concrete interaction examples to make the mechanism felt, not as required implementations.

Distinguish the two offset cases: a non-integer chipped edge is handled by repositioning to the 0 mark, while a scale starting at a whole numeral is handled as end numeral minus start numeral.

Match reteaching to the error: a fencepost or 'start at 1' miscount needs reconnecting numerals to iterated units; an ill-fitting tool choice with sound reading needs the tool-to-scale habit, not re-teaching ruler mechanics.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Measuring with different units
topic.description: Measure the length of an object using two different length units and describe how the measurements relate to the size of the unit chosen
evidence: Measure a desk in both centimetres and inches and compare the two numbers
Explain that measuring with a smaller unit gives a larger number
Predict whether a measurement in centimetres will be greater or less than in inches
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures the same book in centimetres and then in inches, can they explain why the numbers are different even though the book hasn't changed size?

pedagogy.summary: Children measure the SAME object in two different units and discover the inverse relationship: the smaller the unit, the more of them it takes, so the larger the number. Measuring a desk gives ~120 in centimetres but only ~47 in inches — the desk hasn't changed; the count is bigger because a centimetre is smaller than an inch. This is the conceptual bridge from 'counting units' to understanding that a measurement is a number relative to a unit.
bestPractices: Measure one object in two units side by side and put the two numbers next to each other to provoke 'why are they different?'
Make explicit that the object did not change — only the size of the unit did — so a bigger number does not mean a bigger object.
Name the relationship as inverse: smaller unit → more units → bigger number; larger unit → fewer units → smaller number.
Use a same-number/different-unit case (A is 10 small paperclips, B is 10 jumbo paperclips) to show equal counts can mean different lengths.
Ask children to PREDICT which unit will give the bigger number before measuring, so the counterintuitive result confronts a naive prediction.
keyRepresentations: The same desk measured with a cm ruler and an inch ruler, the two counts side by side
Two rows of the same length tiled with small vs large units (many small / few large)
Regular vs jumbo paperclip chains (same count, different length)
A statement frame: 'smaller unit → ____ units → ____ number'
commonMisconceptions: Bigger-unit-bigger-number: believes the larger unit (inch) gives the larger number because inches are 'bigger'.
Thinks the object itself is longer when the number is bigger — the cm measurement 'makes the desk longer'.
Smaller-unit-smaller-number: reasons a centimetre is small so it must give a small number, landing on inches.
Treats equal counts as equal lengths regardless of unit size (10 small clips = 10 jumbo clips).

learn.summary: Children measure the SAME object in two different units and discover the inverse relationship: the smaller the unit, the more of them it takes, so the larger the number. A desk measures about 120 in centimetres but only about 47 in inches — the desk hasn't changed; the count is bigger because a centimetre is smaller than an inch. This bridges from 'counting units' to understanding that a measurement is a number relative to a unit. The ~120/~47 figures are illustrative of one real desk, not fixed for every object.

activities.title: One desk, two rulers: watch the counts differ
feedback: If a learner predicted inches would give the bigger number because 'inches are bigger', re-measure and count both aloud so they watch the smaller centimetre produce MORE units than the inch.
If a learner says the desk is longer in centimetres because the number is bigger, lay both counts against the one unchanged edge and ask what actually changed — only the unit, not the desk.
If a learner reasons 'a centimetre is small so it gives a small number', count centimetres aloud so they feel small units pile up to MORE, not fewer, landing on about 120 vs 47 for this desk.
Confirm success when the learner states centimetres give the bigger number BECAUSE each centimetre is smaller, and predicts metres give a smaller number than centimetres.
activities.rationale: Measuring one unchanged object in two units side by side, with a predict-first step, confronts the naive 'bigger unit means bigger number' prediction against the actual counts; a live tally and a third-unit toggle are proposed to make the inverse relation concrete and generalisable. The draggable rulers, filling tally and metres toggle are optional interaction examples that may make the mechanism visible; they are not required mechanisms, and the approximate counts illustrate one real desk rather than fixed values.
sourceClaims: Second graders learn the inverse relationship between the size of the unit of length and the number of units required: the larger the unit, the fewer units in a given measurement. For example it takes more centimetre lengths than inch lengths to cover a distance because the inch is the larger unit. This is the productive time to measure the same object with different units, both standard and non-standard.

At the Length Unit Relater and Repeater level a child relates the size and number of units (inverse relationship), e.g. 'if you measure with centimeters instead of inches, you'll need more of them, because each one is smaller.'
learnerActions: Before measuring, PREDICT: which number will be bigger when you measure the desk in centimetres versus inches? Say WHY.
Lay the inch ruler along the desk edge and count units as a tally climbs to about 47.
Lay the centimetre ruler along the very same edge and watch the tally race past to about 120.
Point to what actually changed between the two measurements — and confirm the desk itself did not change.
Toggle to a third, larger unit (metres) and watch the count shrink; say whether that fits the rule.
Complete the statement frame: 'smaller unit → ____ units → ____ number' and 'larger unit → ____ units → ____ number'.
activities.intendedInsight: A measurement is a number relative to a unit: the smaller the unit, the more of them fit, so the larger the number — even though the object is unchanged.

activities.title: Same count, different length: the paperclip chains
feedback: If a learner says 10 clips equals 10 clips so the lengths match, lay the chains side by side so the jumbo chain is visibly longer, then name why: each jumbo clip is bigger.
Confirm success when the learner explains the lengths differ because the units differ in size even though the count is the same.
activities.rationale: A same-number/different-unit case directly targets the 'more units = longer' / 'counting means size doesn't matter' bias noted in the progressions, reinforcing that a measurement depends on the unit, not the count alone.
sourceClaims: Students can use the concept of unit to infer relative size: if object A is 10 regular paperclips long and object B is 10 jumbo paperclips long, the number of units is the same but the units differ in size, so the lengths differ. Counting discrete items often convinces students that the size of what is counted does not matter, whereas in measurement unit size is critical, producing a 'more units = longer' bias.
learnerActions: Compare object A, measured as 10 regular paperclips, with object B, measured as 10 jumbo paperclips.
Decide whether the two objects are the same length, and explain why or why not.
Lay the two chains alongside each other to check the prediction.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal counts do NOT mean equal lengths when the units differ in size — unit size is critical in measurement, unlike in counting discrete items.

activities.title: Check and consolidate the inverse relation
feedback: A correct answer with the wrong reason should be probed: a child who truly has the concept says 'centimetres, because a centimetre is smaller so more of them fit', whereas 'inches, because inches are bigger' reveals the direct-relation misconception.
For the metres item, confirm the learner links the larger unit to fewer units and a smaller number, showing the relation generalises in both directions.
Use the labelled side-by-side only as consolidation after the hands-on measuring; on its own it states the idea but does not let the learner generate the counts or predict.
activities.rationale: Predict-and-explain items plus a same-count/different-length item are discriminating checks of the inverse relation because the reason tier catches a correct answer reached by wrong reasoning. The static labelled reference consolidates after generation but cannot elicit prediction or count-generation on its own. The reason-tier discrimination reflects the assessment design rather than a separately source-verified effect.
sourceClaims: Second graders learn the inverse relationship between the size of the unit of length and the number of units required: the larger the unit, the fewer units in a given measurement. For example it takes more centimetre lengths than inch lengths to cover a distance because the inch is the larger unit. This is the productive time to measure the same object with different units, both standard and non-standard.
learnerActions: Answer: which gives the bigger number for the same desk — centimetres or inches — and say why.
Answer: measure the desk in metres instead of centimetres — will the number be bigger or smaller? Why?
Answer the paperclip item: object A is 10 small clips, object B is 10 jumbo clips — same length or not, and why?
Review a side-by-side reference of the desk labelled '120 cm / 47 in' (illustrative of one real desk) and reveal the rule: 'smaller unit → more of them → bigger number'.
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can predict and justify measurement outcomes from unit size across new units, not just recall the desk result.

constraints: The learner must GENERATE the two counts and make a prediction first; a static labelled image (e.g. '120 cm / 47 in' with a tap-to-reveal rule) states the idea but does not let the learner produce the counts or predict, so it belongs as post-activity consolidation rather than the core experience. This describes the affordance of each format, not a claim that other media cannot teach the idea.
Multiple-choice and slider checks can assess the relation, but the reason/explanation must be elicited — a 50/50 answer alone does not show the concept; require the justification tied to unit size.
Make explicit that the object did not change — only the size of the unit did — so a bigger number does not mean a bigger object.
The approximate counts (~120 cm, ~47 in) depend on the specific desk; treat them as illustrative of a real desk, not fixed facts for every object.
Use at least two units spanning different sizes (e.g. inch vs centimetre, then metres) so the relation can be seen to work in both directions.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry rated a 3D interactive as 'adding nothing' and framed dialogue as unable to teach the insight. These are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they are omitted as universal claims. A 2D side-by-side measuring experience is proposed on its narrow affordance (showing two counts on one object), without asserting other media cannot teach this.

Arithmetic/logic self-audit: the inverse relation as stated is correct — a centimetre is smaller than an inch (1 inch ≈ 2.54 cm), so a fixed length yields more centimetres than inches, and metres (larger) yield fewer units than centimetres. The example counts (~120 cm vs ~47 in) are mutually consistent for a desk of roughly 120 cm ≈ 47 in (47 × 2.54 ≈ 119). No arithmetic errors requiring correction were found.

The prerequisite reteach references in the source assessment remain in the assessment field and are not surfaced to learners; they are internal references and should not appear in learner-facing guidance.

The progressions' 'two rows tiled with small vs large units' representation is folded into the measuring activity rather than built as a separate panel; this substitution was not independently re-verified against the source.

assess.poeTask: Before measuring, ask the child to predict which number will be bigger when the desk is measured in centimetres versus inches, and to say WHY. Then have them measure it both ways. The result (about 120 cm but only about 47 inches for the same desk) confronts a 'bigger unit gives a bigger number' prediction; the target explanation, given after observing, is that the centimetre is the smaller unit so it takes more of them.
probeDeeper: You said centimetres gives about 120 and inches about 47 — did the desk get bigger? So what actually changed?
If we measured the same desk in metres instead, would the number be bigger or smaller than the centimetre number? Why?
Object A is 10 small paperclips long and object B is 10 jumbo paperclips long — same number, 10. Are they the same length? Why or why not?
Why does it take MORE centimetres than inches to cover the very same desk?
assess.correctAnswer: The centimetres give the bigger number, because a centimetre is smaller than an inch, so it takes MORE centimetres than inches to cover the same desk (smaller unit → more units → bigger number).

pedagogy.summary: Converting between units means re-expressing one measurement in a different unit of the same attribute (3 km = 3000 m, 2 hours = 120 minutes, 5 weeks = 35 days). The whole procedure hangs on one principle: the smaller the unit, the more of them you need — an inverse relationship between unit size and count — so going from a larger unit to a smaller one multiplies (the number gets bigger). It reinforces place value for the metric system (kilo = 1000) but must NOT be over-applied to time, which runs in 60s and 7s, not powers of ten.
bestPractices: Ground every conversion in the inverse relationship: a km is big, a metre is small, so one km holds MANY metres — hence larger→smaller multiplies and the count rises
Establish the relationships as secure known facts first (1000 m/km, 60 min/hr, 7 days/week), separating metric (base-ten, place value) from time (60s and 7s)
Use a two-column equivalence table so pupils see many equivalents and the pattern (repeated reasoning)
For compound/mixed measures (2 m 30 cm), convert to a common unit BEFORE combining — never string the digits together
Practise both directions and treat multiply/divide as inverse operations
keyRepresentations: A two-column conversion / equivalence table

A '×1000 / ÷1000 machine' making the direction of the operation explicit
A number line or tape diagram for conversion word problems
commonMisconceptions: Converts in the wrong direction — divides when the larger→smaller move should multiply, or expects the smaller-unit answer to be a smaller number
Treats a compound measure like 2 m 30 cm as one number (230, or 2.30) instead of converting and adding
Over-applies base-ten to time — an hour becomes 100 minutes
Doesn't securely know the relationship (uses 100 cm in a km, 30 days in a week)

learn.summary: Pupils (age 8-9) convert between units of the same attribute: 3 km = 3000 m, 2 hours = 120 minutes, 5 weeks = 35 days. The organising principle is the inverse relationship between unit size and count — the smaller the unit, the more of them you need — so moving from a larger unit to a smaller one multiplies and the number gets bigger. Metric conversion builds on base-ten place value (kilo = 1000), but time runs in 60s and 7s and must not be forced into powers of ten. Compound measures (2 m 30 cm) must be converted to a common unit before combining.

activities.title: One length, two scales: seeing why larger→smaller multiplies
feedback: If the learner expects the smaller-unit count to be smaller: point to the two counters — the centimetre count is always ahead of the metre count for the SAME length, because many small units fit inside one large unit.

If the learner picks the wrong gate (÷ for km→m): ask whether 3 km could really be a tiny fraction of a metre; a km is much bigger than a metre, so converting it to metres must give MANY metres (3000 m), not fewer.
If the learner uses the wrong factor (e.g. ×100 for km→m): check which pair it is — cm↔m uses 100, but m↔km uses 1000, because 1 km = 1000 m.
If correct: challenge them to predict the direction AND the factor for an unfamiliar pair before converting, naming which unit is larger.
activities.rationale: The target insight is relational (the inverse size/count relationship) and is made concrete by seeing the same length counted against two different-sized scales with the operation shown as a direction choice. An explicit live recount as the length stretches can make the inverse relationship visible, and a stated wrong-gate check anchors direction; keeping the multiplier tied to the specific pair avoids conflating cm↔m with km↔m.
sourceClaims: The Year 4 Measurement 'Big Idea' for converting units states: 'The smaller the unit, the greater the number of units needed to measure (an inverse relationship between size of unit and measure)' — the principle underlying correct conversion direction.

Year 4 pupils are taught to 'convert between different units of measure [for example, kilometre to metre; hour to minute]' and to 'solve problems involving converting from hours to minutes, minutes to seconds, years to months, weeks to days'; non-statutory guidance says they 'use multiplication to convert from larger to smaller units' and build on place value and decimal notation.

Conversion reinforces place value: 'kilo' means a thousand so 3000 m = 3 km; a kilometre is a 'unit of units' (1000 metres); and the documented root difficulty is the inverse size/count relationship (2.MD.2) — children count units and assign cardinality, arguing a row of 6 matches is 'longer' than a row of fewer larger matches.
learnerActions: Look at one physical length laid against two scales stacked together — e.g. a metre scale and a centimetre scale — each with its own counter showing how many of that unit fit the length
Make the length longer and watch BOTH counts rise, then say which count rises faster and which is always the bigger number

Explain in your own words why the smaller unit always gives the bigger count (one large unit holds many small units, so the multiplier equals how many small units fit one large unit — e.g. 100 cm in a metre)

Feed a value through a '×/÷' gate to convert between a larger and a smaller unit and back; use the km↔m case where the factor is ×1000/÷1000 because 1 km = 1000 m, and note that a different pair has a different factor (100 for cm per m)
Deliberately pick the wrong gate once and describe why the answer is an absurd size (e.g. 3 km wrongly divided to 0.003 m)
State the rule you observed: larger unit → fewer, larger units; smaller unit → more units, so larger→smaller multiplies
activities.intendedInsight: Why larger→smaller multiplies: because a larger unit holds many of the smaller unit, the smaller-unit count is always the bigger number — the inverse relationship between unit size and count, observed rather than memorised. The exact multiplier depends on the pair (100 for cm↔m, 1000 for m↔km).

activities.title: Known-facts reference: metric vs time
feedback: If the learner answers 2 hours = 200 minutes: an hour is 60 minutes, not 100 — time does not use powers of ten, so multiply by 60 (2 × 60 = 120).
If the learner uses 100 m in a km or 30 days in a week: check the reference — 1000 m in a km, 7 days in a week.
If the learner says 90 cm > 1 m because 90 > 1: the units differ; 1 m = 100 cm, so 90 cm is less than 1 m.
activities.rationale: Direction reasoning only works if the specific relationship is known, so establishing the facts first — and separating base-ten metric from time's 60s and 7s — prevents the common error of over-applying place value to time. A tap-to-reveal prefix chart can teach the facts and base-ten structure, though it cannot itself demonstrate the multiply/divide direction dynamic.

learnerActions: Build and keep a reference of the relationships as secure known facts: 1000 m = 1 km, 60 seconds = 1 minute, 60 minutes = 1 hour, 7 days = 1 week
Sort the facts into two groups — metric (base-ten, follows place value: kilo = 1000) and time (60s and 7s, NOT powers of ten)
Reveal the meaning of metric prefixes (e.g. kilo = 1000, centi = one hundredth) and tie each to a worked equivalent
Answer 'which is bigger, 90 cm or 1 m?' and explain how you know, so a bigger number does not fool you
Test yourself: 'How many minutes in 2 hours?' — then explain why the answer is 120, not 100
activities.intendedInsight: Correct conversion depends on knowing the right relationship securely, and on recognising that time is not base-ten; metric and time must be kept separate.

activities.title: Compound measures: convert before combining
feedback: If the learner writes 230 straight away as if stringing digits: it works here only because 2 m = 200 cm; have them show the conversion step so they don't generalise the shortcut wrongly.

If the learner writes 2.30 cm or another mixed-up number: this treats the two units as one number; convert 2 m to 200 cm first, then add 30 cm = 230 cm (writing 2.30 m is also correct, but only with the metre unit).
If the learner adds 2 + 30 = 32 across units: 2 m and 30 cm are different units; turn the metres into centimetres before adding.
activities.rationale: Mastery tasks that refuse to total until both parts share a unit surface the compound-measure-as-single-number error, forcing the conversion step to become explicit. A builder showing the parts as blocks that won't add up until both are the same unit can make this concrete.
sourceClaims: Year 5 mastery tasks deliberately require converting mixed/compound measures to a common unit rather than combining bare numbers, e.g. the true/false task '32 cm + 1.05 m = 150 cm − 0.13 m' and combining ribbons of '1.2 m' and '90 cm' — tasks that surface the compound-measure-as-single-number error.

learnerActions: Write 2 m 30 cm all in centimetres: convert the metres first (2 m = 200 cm), then add the 30 cm to get 230 cm — explaining each step
Notice that adding the numbers across units (2 + 30 = 32) or writing 2.30 cm does NOT give the length; say why (2.30 m is a correct way to write it, but only with the metre unit)
Work a mixed set and check equivalences, e.g. decide true/false for '32 cm + 1.05 m = 150 cm − 0.13 m' by converting everything to one unit first
Combine two lengths given in different units, e.g. a '1.2 m' ribbon and a '90 cm' ribbon, by converting to a common unit before adding
activities.intendedInsight: A compound measure like 2 m 30 cm is not a single number; its parts must be converted to a common unit before they can be combined.

activities.title: Both-directions conversion practice targeting common errors
feedback: If the learner divides for km→m (gives 0.003 m): a km is the larger unit, so it holds many metres — multiply (3 × 1000 = 3000 m).
If the learner multiplies for m→km: going to a larger unit means fewer, larger units — divide.
If the learner hesitates on the factor: check the known-facts reference and confirm whether the pair is metric (place value) or time (60s/7s).
activities.rationale: Conversion is a fluency procedure, and the signature errors (wrong direction, smaller-answer expectation, base-ten-for-time) make natural wrong-answer traps for learners to notice and correct during practice and self-checking. Practising both directions treats multiply/divide as inverses. Recognition-style items (spotting a wrong answer) check judgement but do not by themselves elicit independent construction, so pair them with items where the learner performs and explains the conversion.

Year 4 pupils are taught to 'convert between different units of measure [for example, kilometre to metre; hour to minute]' and to 'solve problems involving converting from hours to minutes, minutes to seconds, years to months, weeks to days'; non-statutory guidance says they 'use multiplication to convert from larger to smaller units' and build on place value and decimal notation.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in conversions in both directions: '3 km = ___ m' and '3000 m = ___ km'
Spot the wrong-direction answer, e.g. decide whether '3 km = 300 m' is right and correct it
Match equivalent measures across units and sort cards into groups of equal value
Convert 5 weeks to days and 2 hours to minutes, naming the factor used each time

activities.intendedInsight: Conversion is a two-way fluency procedure: multiply and divide are inverse operations, and direction is chosen by which unit is larger.

constraints: Establish the conversion relationships (1000 m/km, 60 s/min, 60 min/hr, 7 days/week) as secure known facts before drilling the procedure; a facts reference can stay to hand while the conversion direction is the focus.
Keep metric (base-ten, place value) separate from time (60s and 7s); do not over-apply powers of ten to time (an hour is 60 minutes, not 100).
The conversion multiplier is pair-specific (100 for cm↔m, 1000 for m↔km); do not let one example's factor be carried onto a different unit pair.

For compound/mixed measures, convert to a common unit BEFORE combining; never allow digits from different units to be strung together (2 m 30 cm ≠ 230 by juxtaposition — it equals 230 cm only after converting 2 m to 200 cm).

A static prefix/place-value chart with tap-to-reveal can teach the facts and base-ten structure, but pre-set content cannot itself run the live multiply/divide direction demonstration; use it as a facts scaffold, not as the main vehicle for the direction insight.
Recognition-only items (e.g. spotting a wrong conversion) assess judgement; include items where the learner constructs and explains a conversion to elicit independent production.

The manipulable two-scale demonstration is one effective way to make the inverse relationship visible; it is a proposal, not the only route — physical rulers, equivalence tables, and number lines can also make differing counts and conversion steps concrete.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles rather than proving any activity was tested.

The source's non-preferred artefact entries were preserved as alternatives: the prefix/place-value chart (kept as the known-facts scaffold, with its stated limit that it cannot run the direction dynamic) and the practice item types (folded into both-directions practice). The entries judged poor fit (3D interactive, in-role conversation) were dropped as not the vehicle for a numeric/relational procedure; this reflects a fit judgement and should not be read as a universal law that such media 'teach nothing'.

The original demonstration conflated cm/m scales with a km↔m ×1000 gate; this has been corrected by making the multiplier pair-specific (100 for cm↔m, 1000 for m↔km) in the activity, insight and feedback.

Self-audit of arithmetic and examples: 3 × 1000 = 3000 m ✓; 2 × 60 = 120 min ✓; 5 × 7 = 35 days ✓; 2 m = 200 cm, + 30 cm = 230 cm ✓; 1 m = 100 cm so 90 cm < 1 m ✓; wrong-gate 3 ÷ 1000 = 0.003 m shown only as an absurd error to correct. The source's own flagged errors (division giving 0.003 m, 200 min, 100 cm per km, 30 days per week) are retained only as error patterns to correct, not as valid answers.

The source's true/false equivalence task '32 cm + 1.05 m = 150 cm − 0.13 m' was kept verbatim as a mastery-style task; its truth value was not independently re-solved here — left to the teacher to verify when used (both sides appear to convert to 137 cm, so it reads TRUE, but confirm before relying on it).

Narrow affordance, not a universal law: for this numeric/relational conversion procedure an in-role dialogue partner is not itself the vehicle for performing and checking the calculations, and an added third dimension is not needed to make the inverse size/count relationship visible. These are fit judgements for media choice, not claims that such media teach nothing.

probeDeeper: 'You multiplied to turn km into m. How would you turn 3000 m back into km — and why does the operation flip?'
'Sam says 90 cm must be longer than 1 m because 90 is bigger than 1. What would you tell Sam?' (counterexample targeting the larger-number confusion)

pedagogy.summary: Year 5 (age 9–10) pupils learn the relative sizes of metric units (km/m/cm/mm, kg/g, l/ml) and convert between them, expressing a measurement in terms of a smaller unit and recording equivalents in conversion tables. Conversion is APPLIED place value: to a smaller unit you multiply (there are more of them); to a larger unit you divide (fewer of them). The two persistent hazards are choosing the wrong operation and manipulating zeros/decimals mechanically ('add a zero') instead of moving the digits across a fixed decimal point.
bestPractices: Anchor the multiply/divide decision in REASONING about unit size, not a rule: 'which unit is bigger? there are fewer of the bigger unit, so to reach it I divide' — the rule is exactly what pupils reverse (Oak National Academy).

Teach conversion as multiplying/dividing by 10, 100, 1000, and talk about the DIGITS moving (one/two/three places) while the decimal point stays fixed — never 'move the decimal point' or 'add a zero' (NCETM Spine 2.29).
Secure fluency with ×/÷ by 10/100/1000 BEFORE layering on conversion, to avoid overload.
Use a place-value chart / Gattegno chart so pupils SEE the digits shift and the value change (the 1 in 1.75 km becomes the 1 thousand in 1750 m).

Build conversion tables and read them as a set of equivalent multiplications; include mixed-unit forms (2 kg 350 g = 2350 g) and always add a reasonableness check (bigger or smaller number than we started with?).
keyRepresentations: Place-value / Gattegno chart showing digits sliding across a fixed decimal point

commonMisconceptions: Confuses when to multiply and when to divide (converts to a smaller unit by dividing, or vice versa).
