Treats a mixed unit as concatenation (2 kg 35 g → '235 g'), a two-separate-numbers error.
Fills a conversion table by copying a pattern without understanding the ×10 relationship.

learn.summary: Year 5 pupils (age 9–10) learn the relative sizes of units within one system (metric km/m/cm/mm, kg/g, l/ml; and time units hr/min/sec, which are not metric) and convert between metric units, expressing a measurement in a smaller unit and recording equivalents in conversion tables. Metric conversion is applied place value: converting to a SMALLER unit means multiplying (there are more of them); converting to a LARGER unit means dividing (there are fewer of them). The two persistent hazards are choosing the wrong operation and manipulating zeros/decimals mechanically ('add a zero') instead of moving the digits across a fixed decimal point. The core activity is a live place-value transformation where digits slide across a fixed point, supported by table-building, mixed-unit recomposition, and targeted practice that probes direction and zero errors. (Note: the digit-sliding by 10/100/1000 applies to the metric units; hr/min/sec relate by ×60 and are included only in the 'relative sizes' knowledge.)

activities.title: Slide the digits across a fixed decimal point
feedback: If the pupil appends a zero (3.5 km → '3.50 m') or uses the wrong factor (3.5 km → '350 m', i.e. ×100), show the digits' positions on the chart: ×1000 moves each digit three places left past a fixed point, so 3.5 lands as 3500.
If direction is reversed (3.5 km → 0.0035 m), re-ask 'metres are smaller, so are there more or fewer than 3.5?' — more, so multiply, so the answer is bigger than 3.5.
Add a reasonableness check every time: 'Is your answer bigger or smaller than you started with, and does that fit the unit size?'
activities.rationale: Anchoring the multiply/divide choice in reasoning about unit size targets the exact rule pupils reverse, and showing digit movement across a fixed point addresses why 'add a zero' breaks with decimals. A live, interactive chart (type a value, choose a unit, see digits slide and point stay fixed) is proposed to make the transformation felt rather than told; a static reference table can show one worked conversion but does not let the pupil perform the operation or see the digits move.
sourceClaims: To multiply by 10/100/1000 the DIGITS move one/two/three places left (right to divide) while the decimal point stays fixed; measures are converted using multiplication and division by 10/100/1000; 'add/remove a zero' reasoning is false for decimals (e.g. 25.34×10 ≠ 25.340).
Pupils confuse when to multiply and when to divide when converting; the recommended fix is to reason about unit size — there are fewer of the larger unit, so converting to it means dividing.
learnerActions: Enter a measurement such as 3.5 km and choose the target unit (metres).
Before computing, answer the prompt: 'Is a metre bigger or smaller than a kilometre — so will there be MORE metres or FEWER?' State whether this means multiply or divide.

Watch (or physically move, using a place-value chart or Gattegno chart) every digit slide three places left while the decimal point stays nailed in place, so 3.5 becomes 3500, with place-holder zeros dropping in where needed.
Repeat for a case that keeps the decimal visible, e.g. 1.75 km to m, naming where each digit lands (the 1 becomes 1 thousand, giving 1750 m).
Do at least one divide case too, e.g. 4500 m to km, moving digits three places right to give 4.5 km.
activities.intendedInsight: The number grows (or shrinks) because the DIGITS move a fixed number of places, not because zeros are 'added' — so 3.5 km can never become 3.50 m.

activities.title: Build and check conversion tables
feedback: If a pupil pattern-copies without the ×10 idea, ask what single multiplication turns the left column into the right (auto-checking each row against ×10 makes a broken row visible immediately).
Correct answers for the cm→mm table: 1→10, 2→20, 5→50, 10→100.
activities.rationale: Reading tables as equivalent multiplications ties table completion back to the underlying factor, countering mechanical copying. Direction and factor practice map cleanly onto fill-in and matching tasks and can systematically probe the add-a-zero and direction errors, though such practice gives no live digit-movement.
sourceClaims: To multiply by 10/100/1000 the DIGITS move one/two/three places left (right to divide) while the decimal point stays fixed; measures are converted using multiplication and division by 10/100/1000; 'add/remove a zero' reasoning is false for decimals (e.g. 25.34×10 ≠ 25.340).
learnerActions: Complete a cm→mm table: 1→__, 2→__, 5→__, 10→__ and say what you multiply by for each row.
Read the completed table aloud as a set of equivalent multiplications ('each centimetre is ten millimetres — I'm multiplying by 10').
Check each row against the ×10 relationship and flag any row that breaks the pattern, explaining why it is wrong.
Build a second table for a different pair of units (e.g. kg→g, ×1000) to see the same structure with a different multiplier.
activities.intendedInsight: A conversion table is a repeated multiplication by the same factor, not a copied number pattern — understanding the factor lets you extend or correct any row.

activities.title: Recompose a mixed unit into one smaller unit
feedback: If the pupil concatenates (2 kg 35 g → '235 g'), show 2 kg = 2000 g on a place-value chart or bar and add 35, exposing the empty hundreds place: 2035 g.
Confirm 2 kg 350 g = 2350 g because 2000 + 350 = 2350 (the digits of 350 happen to fill all three lower places, which is why this case hides the error that 2 kg 35 g reveals).
activities.rationale: Mixed-unit concatenation is a whole-number 'two separate numbers' error; recomposing via place value and testing a case where the loose amount has fewer digits forces attention to the empty place-value columns.
sourceClaims: Children commonly treat a mixed measurement (or a decimal) as two separate whole numbers — e.g. '2 m and 30 cm' rather than 230 cm — driven by whole-number language.
learnerActions: Express 2 kg 350 g as a number of grams, showing the step 2 kg = 2000 g, then 2000 + 350 = 2350 g.
Test the tricky case 2 kg 35 g: decide whether it equals 235 g or 2035 g and justify using place value.
Use a bar (2 kg + loose grams recomposed as one quantity) to make the missing hundreds place visible when the loose amount is small.
State a check: the combined gram total must include the thousands from the kilograms.
activities.intendedInsight: A mixed unit is recomposed by converting the larger part and ADDING, not by writing the two numbers side by side — so 2 kg 35 g = 2035 g, not 235 g.

activities.title: Choose and justify the operation before calculating
feedback: If justification is only 'that's the rule', redirect to unit size: which unit is bigger, so are there more or fewer of the target unit?
For the true/false item: 25.34 × 10 = 253.4, NOT 25.340 — appending a zero does not multiply a decimal by 10; the digits move one place left.
activities.rationale: Requiring a stated justification before computing surfaces rule-guessing and builds the unit-size reasoning that fixes direction; true/false items on the zero error make the decimal failure explicit.

learnerActions: For a mix of conversions (some to smaller units, some to larger), first state 'multiply' or 'divide' and why, using unit size, BEFORE working the answer.

constraints: Secure fluency with ×/÷ by 10, 100 and 1000 BEFORE layering on conversion, to avoid overload.
Talk about the DIGITS moving one/two/three places while the decimal point stays fixed; never say 'move the decimal point' or 'add a zero'.

Practice tasks (fill-in conversions, matching equivalents, choose-the-operation items) are a strong companion for probing direction and zero errors but provide no live digit-movement feedback; pair them with the place-value chart work, which shows the transformation.
A static reference table or single worked example can show a result but does not let the pupil perform the conversion or watch digits move; treat it as reference only, not the main teaching vehicle.

A place-value slider/chart where digits visibly slide across a fixed point is proposed as a strong vehicle for THIS numeric transformation; it is not claimed superior for every topic. The content here is numeric, so 3D or spatial representations add little for this particular conversion skill.

Recognition-only responses (picking a correct conversion from options) do not by themselves show the pupil can independently reason about direction or move the digits; include tasks requiring them to produce and justify the conversion.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit checks performed: 3.5 km = 3500 m (×1000) is correct; 1.75 km = 1750 m; 4500 m = 4.5 km; cm→mm table 1→10, 2→20, 5→50, 10→100 is correct; 2 kg 350 g = 2350 g and 2 kg 35 g = 2035 g are correct; 25.34 × 10 = 253.4 (not 25.340) is correct. No arithmetic errors found in the migrated examples.

The original source listed one evidence-table row set as 1→10, 2→20, 3→30 while the assessment used 1,2,5,10 (→10,20,50,100); activities use 1,2,5,10 consistently. No conflict in the ×10 relationship, only in which rows are shown.

Some underlying sources were marked unverified (Oak National Academy guidance; DfE programmes of study) in the original row; their claims are retained as cited but their verification status is unchanged.

All four original misconceptions are covered: direction confusion, 'add a zero', mixed-unit concatenation, and pattern-copying a table without the ×10 factor (the last via the table-builder's auto-check and the 'read the table as equivalent multiplications' action).
The double-number-line representation from the original keyRepresentations is not reflected in any activity; the bar model and place-value/Gattegno chart are used instead.

probeDeeper: 'Metres are smaller than kilometres — so should the number of metres be bigger or smaller than 3.5? Does your answer fit?'
'You wrote 3.5 km = ___ m. If I said 3.50 m, would that be right? Why not?'

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiply/divide direction confusion — converts to a smaller unit by dividing (or to a larger unit by multiplying) because the operation is a memorised rule, not reasoning about unit size (e.g. 3.5 km → 0.0035 m).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reason from unit size every time: 'metres are smaller than kilometres, so there are MORE of them — multiply.' Rehearse the 'fewer of the bigger unit → divide' heuristic before any calculation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The answer is smaller when it should be bigger (or vice versa); the child cannot say why they multiplied or divided beyond 'that's the rule'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Add a zero' / mechanical zeros — multiplies by 1000 by appending zeros, which breaks with the decimal: 3.5 km → '350 m' (one zero) or '3.50 m'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Switch to digit-movement on a place-value chart: to ×1000 the digits move three places LEFT past a fixed point; use true/false items (25.34×10 = 25.340?) to expose why 'add a zero' fails for decimals.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A converted value with the wrong number of digits after (or before) the point; zeros tacked on rather than digits moved three places.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mixed-unit concatenation — treats 2 kg 350 g as digits to string together, so a case like 2 kg 35 g becomes '235 g' instead of 2035 g (a two-separate-numbers error).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recompose via place value: 2 kg = 2000 g, then add the loose grams; show 2 kg 35 g ≠ 235 g on a bar so the missing hundreds place is visible.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Recomposing a mixed unit by writing the two numbers side by side rather than adding 2000 g + 35 g.

responseLevels.gap: Guesses the operation, appends/removes zeros mechanically, and concatenates mixed units; a converted value with the wrong size.
responseLevels.full: Reasons from unit size to choose ×/÷, moves the digits correctly (including decimals) across a fixed point, recomposes mixed units into one smaller unit, and completes/reads conversion tables — transferring across length, mass and capacity.
responseLevels.partial: Converts a whole-number case in one direction but reverses direction the other way, mishandles the decimal in 3.5 km, or fills the table by pattern-copying without the ×10 idea.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three tasks and ask them to think aloud: (1) 'Convert 3.5 km to metres.' (2) 'Complete this cm→mm table: 1→__, 2→__, 5→__, 10→__.' (3) 'Write 2 kg 350 g as a number of grams.' Each time ask 'did you multiply or divide, and how did you know?' Watch the direction reasoning and how they handle the digits/zeros — not just the answers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil who understands converts 3.5 km to 3500 m and justifies by unit size; a pupil who doesn't either divides (0.0035 m) or 'adds a zero' (350 m / 3.50 m), and may concatenate 2 kg 350 g wrongly for a case like 2 kg 35 g. Reasoning-from-unit-size versus rule-guessing diverge exactly on the direction and on the decimal case.

topic.description: Understand and use approximate equivalences between metric units and common imperial units (inches, pounds, pints)
evidence: State that 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm and use this to estimate length in inches

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that a baby weighs 7 pounds, can they give a rough idea of that in kilograms — using the approximate conversion they know?

pedagogy.summary: By Year 5 children know metric units well; the goal here is a working, APPROXIMATE sense of common imperial units through the key facts 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm, 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb and 1 litre ≈ 1.75 pints, used to estimate and to judge whether an answer is sensible. Children meet the symbol ≈ and the idea that these equivalences are approximate — indeed among the common facts inch↔cm is genuinely approximate, while relationships purely within imperial (pound↔ounce, pint↔gallon) are exact. Teaching leans on dual scales and familiar referent objects so the equivalence is felt, and on estimation ('about how many…') rather than exact calculation.
bestPractices: Introduce ≈ explicitly and contrast 'approximately equal' with 'equal'; expect answers phrased as 'about …'.

Anchor each fact to a familiar referent (a 30 cm ruler ≈ 12 inches; a bag of sugar ≈ 2.2 lb; a large bottle ≈ 1.75 pints) and to a dual-scale tool (ruler with inches and cm; kitchen scales showing kg and lb).
Use a double number line or ratio table so the constant multiplicative relationship is visible and children scale up (2 inches ≈ 5 cm) rather than treat each conversion in isolation.
Emphasise which unit is the larger, and therefore whether the count of units should be more or fewer after converting; use estimation to sense-check direction.
Pre-teach imperial vocabulary (inch, foot, pound, ounce, stone, pint, gallon), since many children have little prior exposure to these units.
keyRepresentations: Dual-scale ruler (inches and cm side by side)
Kitchen/bathroom scales showing kg and lb together
Double number line
Ratio / conversion table
Familiar referent objects (sugar bag, ruler, bottle)
commonMisconceptions: Treats an approximate equivalence as exact (writes 1 inch = 2.5 cm and cannot say the answer is only roughly right).
Confuses which unit is larger, so converts in the wrong direction (multiplies when they should divide, or vice versa) because the larger number of cm suggests a cm is the bigger unit.
Struggles with unfamiliar imperial vocabulary and relationships (e.g. knows feet and inches measure length but not that 1 foot = 12 inches).

learn.summary: Builds a working, approximate sense of common imperial units through key facts (1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm, 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb, 1 litre ≈ 1.75 pints) used for estimation and sense-checking. Learners meet the ≈ symbol and the idea that these cross-system facts are used only roughly: the conversion factors are fixed but rounded for everyday use (e.g. 2.54→2.5, 2.20462→2.2, 1.75975→1.75), so answers are phrased as 'about …'. Relationships purely within imperial — pound↔ounce, stone↔pound, gallon↔pint, foot↔inch — are exact. Teaching anchors each fact to a familiar referent object and a dual scale, emphasises which unit is larger (and hence whether the count goes up or down), and treats conversion as scaling a constant multiplicative ratio rather than isolated one-off sums. Includes a hands-on/tool-based estimation activity, a static dual-scale fact activity, a check-and-practice activity, and vocabulary support; each with a distinct purpose and limits.

activities.title: Dual-scale estimation playground
feedback: If the learner expects a fixed add-on rather than a multiplier, show 1 kg → ~2.2 lb and 3 kg → ~6.6 lb and ask what stays constant (the ×2.2 ratio, not the gap).
If they insist the everyday value is exact, reveal the fuller figure (e.g. 2.20462 lb) and contrast with a tidy within-system fact like 100 cm = 1 m.
Praise estimates phrased as 'about 2.2 lb' and reasoning that both scales move together by the same ratio.
activities.rationale: A tool that recomputes both scales as the learner acts makes the constant multiplier visible and ties estimation to a familiar referent, supporting the required approximate equivalences. The live dial, double number line, ratio table and 'is it exact?' toggle are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory components, and the tool is a proposed approach rather than a validated or uniquely effective one.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory: 'understand and use approximate equivalences between metric units and common imperial units such as inches, pounds and pints.'

Facts taught: 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm; the inch↔cm conversion is approximate while pound↔ounce, stone↔pound and gallon↔pint relationships are exact; children have less prior experience of imperial measures so meet a lot of new vocabulary.
learnerActions: Place a bag of sugar (about 1 kg) on a kitchen scale reading kilograms, then estimate its weight in pounds before checking.
Drag a pointer on a blank pounds dial to your estimate, then reveal the true value and compare it against a double number line showing 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb.
Load 3 kg and watch both scales climb together; describe in words how the pounds number relates to the kg number (about 2.2 times), with a ratio/conversion table recording each kg–lb pair.
Use a ruler tool that overlays inches on centimetres: line up 1 inch and read off that it spans about 2.5 cm, then scale up (2 inches ≈ 5 cm).
Toggle 'is it exact?' to reveal the fuller value (e.g. 1 kg ≈ 2.20462 lb) and explain why the everyday answer is only 'about'.
activities.intendedInsight: Converting between systems means scaling by a fixed multiplier (pounds ≈ 2.2 × kg; inches ≈ cm ÷ 2.5), and because the taught factor is rounded the cross-system answer is used approximately, so it is phrased as 'about …'.

activities.title: Dual-scale fact set with referent objects
feedback: If the learner reads ≈ as =, point to the symbol and restate it as 'is about'.
If they cannot scale a fact beyond the stated one, prompt them to double the referent and the number together.
Confirm correct recall and encourage connecting each fact to its object.
activities.rationale: A static dual-scale display with tap-to-reveal facts efficiently conveys the fact set and referents. Because it does not recompute, scaling up must be prompted verbally rather than felt, so it is well suited as a reference/introduction stage before hands-on scaling, without implying a static display cannot support learning.
sourceClaims: Facts taught: 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm; the inch↔cm conversion is approximate while pound↔ounce, stone↔pound and gallon↔pint relationships are exact; children have less prior experience of imperial measures so meet a lot of new vocabulary.
learnerActions: Look at a dual-scale ruler (inches and cm side by side) and read off that a 30 cm ruler is about 12 inches.
Match familiar referent objects to facts: a 1 kg bag of sugar ≈ 2.2 lb; a 1-litre bottle ≈ 1.75 pints; an adult's thumb-width ≈ 1 inch (a child's is usually a bit narrower).
Tap each ≈ fact to reveal and read it aloud, saying 'about' each time.
After reading a fact, say aloud how you would scale it up (e.g. two bags of sugar ≈ 4.4 lb) even though the display does not recompute.
activities.intendedInsight: The key approximate equivalences become memorable when tied to objects you can picture and to a scale where both unit systems sit side by side.

activities.title: Estimate and sense-check practice
feedback: If a learner answers about 37.5 inches for 15 cm (15 × 2.5), that is the wrong-direction error: an inch is longer than a cm, so there must be FEWER inches than cm — about 6 (15 ÷ 2.5). Put a dual-scale ruler in their hands and mark 1 inch against the cm side.
If a learner gives about 6 inches but calls it exact, show that a real 6-inch length is a little over 15 cm, so 1 inch is a bit more than 2.5 cm.
Confirm estimates phrased as 'about' with a correct direction and a reasonable size.
activities.rationale: Slider and multiple-choice checks are well suited to confirming recall of the facts and sense-of-size, and the wrong-direction error gives a natural distractor. This checks and rehearses the facts but does not by itself build the multiplicative feel, so pair it with hands-on scaling; a check does not inherently preclude understanding.
learnerActions: Estimate on a slider: 'A 10 kg dog is about ___ lb' (expect about 22 lb).
Answer 'About how many inches is 15 cm?' and justify the direction of conversion.
Choose which unit is larger — 1 inch or 1 cm — and say whether the count of inches should be more or fewer than the count of cm.
Decide whether 2 kg of flour is more or fewer pounds than 2, and give a rough figure (about 4.4 lb).
activities.intendedInsight: Estimating and checking whether an answer is sensible relies on knowing which unit is larger and therefore which direction the count moves.

activities.title: Imperial vocabulary familiarisation
feedback: If a learner stalls or confuses inches and feet, treat it as lack of exposure, not a misconception: scaffold with real objects and referents, then re-ask.
Reinforce that within-imperial facts (12 inches = 1 foot) are exact, unlike the cross-system facts that use rounded conversion factors.
activities.rationale: Many learners have little prior exposure to imperial measures and meet a lot of new vocabulary, so pre-teaching names and referents removes a barrier that can look like a conceptual error. It also sets up the exact-vs-approximate distinction.
sourceClaims: Facts taught: 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm; the inch↔cm conversion is approximate while pound↔ounce, stone↔pound and gallon↔pint relationships are exact; children have less prior experience of imperial measures so meet a lot of new vocabulary.
learnerActions: Meet and say the imperial unit names: inch, foot, pound, ounce, stone, pint, gallon.
Match each unit to what it measures (length, mass or capacity) and to a familiar referent (an adult's thumb-width ≈ 1 inch; foot-long ruler = 12 inches).
Learn the exact within-imperial relationships (1 foot = 12 inches; 16 ounces = 1 pound) and contrast them with the approximate cross-system facts.
Re-attempt an estimation question after building familiarity.
activities.intendedInsight: Imperial units are often unfamiliar; knowing the names, what they measure, and the exact relationships within imperial supports confident estimation without a false belief getting in the way.

constraints: Introduce ≈ explicitly and contrast 'approximately equal' with 'equal'; expect and accept answers phrased as 'about …'.

Keep clear that the taught cross-system facts (inch↔cm, kg↔lb, litre↔pint) are all used approximately — their conversion factors are fixed but rounded for everyday use — while relationships purely within imperial (pound↔ounce, stone↔pound, gallon↔pint, foot↔inch) are exact.
Emphasise which unit is larger before converting, so learners judge whether the count should be more or fewer and avoid multiplying when they should divide.
Static dual-scale displays convey facts and referents but do not let the learner feel scaling; use them as reference or introduction rather than the sole route to the multiplicative idea.
Slider/multiple-choice practice checks recall and sense-of-size but does not on its own build the multiplicative feel; pair it with hands-on or tool-based scaling.
Target is a working approximate sense for estimation and sense-checking, not exact arithmetic conversion.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Worked-example check: 15 cm ÷ 2.5 = 6 inches (correct); the wrong-direction distractor 15 × 2.5 = 37.5 inches is flagged as an error, not a valid answer (the original row rounded this to 37). 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb gives 10 kg ≈ 22 lb and 3 kg ≈ 6.6 lb; 2 kg ≈ 4.4 lb (all correct).

The legacy row rated 3D and dialogue as adding 'nothing'/'little'; these universal comparative claims are not established by catalog ratings and have been omitted rather than asserted. The dual-scale/tool approach is offered as a well-matched proposal, not the only way to teach approximate equivalence.
The stated value 1 kg ≈ 2.20462 lb is a conventional figure; treat as illustrative for the 'is it exact?' point rather than independently verified here.

Strictly, 1 inch = 2.54 cm, 1 kg = 2.20462 lb and 1 litre ≈ 1.75975 pints are exact (defined) conversions; the Year 5 approximation lies in using the rounded factors 2.5, 2.2 and 1.75. The original row's wording singling out inch↔cm as uniquely 'genuinely approximate' among the cross-system facts has been corrected to treat all three uniformly as rounded-factor approximations, while keeping the curriculum framing of 'approximate equivalences'.

probeDeeper: If a friend said 15 cm is EXACTLY 6 inches, would you agree? Why might it not be exactly 6?
A ruler shows 12 inches on one edge and 30 cm on the other. Which is the longer unit, 1 inch or 1 cm — and how does the ruler show you?
Your pencil was about 6 inches. Now a rope is 250 cm — about how many inches, and is the same rule working?
A bag of flour is 2 kg. Is that more or fewer than 2 pounds, and roughly how many pounds?
assess.correctAnswer: About 6 inches, reasoning that each inch is about 2.5 cm, so 15 cm splits into 6 lots of 2.5 (15 ÷ 2.5 = 6); and stating it is only approximate because 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm is not exact.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses which unit is larger and converts the wrong way ('a cm is bigger, so there must be more inches') — multiplies by 2.5 instead of dividing.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put a dual-scale ruler in their hands and mark 1 inch against the cm side: one inch spans about two-and-a-half cm, so an inch is longer and there must be fewer inches than cm. Re-establish relative unit size before converting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers about 37 inches (15 × 2.5), giving MORE inches than cm.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the approximate equivalence as exact — reads ≈ as = and cannot say the answer is only roughly right.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show ≈ means 'about'; measure a real 6-inch length against a cm ruler and note it is a little over 15 cm, so 1 inch is a bit more than 2.5 cm. Contrast an exact metric conversion (100 cm = 1 m) with this approximate one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes '15 cm = 6 inches' and, when asked if it is exactly 6, insists it is exact; unable to explain ≈.

errorPatterns.pattern: Unfamiliar with imperial units and their names, so hesitates or misuses vocabulary rather than holding a wrong belief.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold with real objects and referents (thumb-width ≈ 1 inch, foot-long ruler = 12 inches) rather than reteaching; build familiarity, then re-ask.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Knows inches measure length but is unsure how big an inch is, or confuses inches/feet; stalls for lack of exposure, not because of a false idea.

responseLevels.gap: Guesses, or applies the fact the wrong way (e.g. 15 × 2.5 ≈ 37), showing no sense of which unit is larger or that 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm.
responseLevels.full: Divides or scales correctly to about 6 inches, states the answer is approximate, justifies that an inch is the larger unit so there are fewer inches than cm, and transfers the rule to a new length or to a mass/capacity equivalence.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm and reaches about 6 inches, but cannot explain why it is division/scaling, or treats the answer as exact; lists the equivalence facts without connecting them to which unit is larger.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A pencil is 15 cm long. Roughly how many inches is that — and explain how you worked it out. (You know 1 inch is about 2.5 cm.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child reasoning correctly divides (or scales the ratio down) and gets ~6 inches — fewer inches than cm because an inch is the larger unit. A child who thinks a cm is larger than an inch converts the wrong way and multiplies (15 × 2.5 ≈ 37 inches), a very different answer. A child who has only memorised the fact gives ~6 but cannot justify the direction or that it is approximate.

topic.description: Convert among different-sized standard measurement units within a given system (e.g. 5 cm to 0.05 m) using decimal notation to up to three decimal places; convert between smaller and larger units of length, mass, volume, and time
evidence: Convert 3,250 g to 3.25 kg using decimal notation
Convert 0.45 km to 450 m
Explain the relationship between mm, cm, m, and km using powers of 10
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to convert 5 cm to metres and write the answer as a decimal, can they do it — and also convert 2.45 kg into grams?

pedagogy.summary: Year 6 (age 10–11) pupils convert between standard units using DECIMAL notation to up to three decimal places, moving in both directions (smaller↔larger), and can explain the mm–cm–m–km (and g–kg, ml–l) relationships as powers of 10. This is the decimal extension of Year 5 conversion: the same 'reason from unit size, move the digits' method, now with the decimal point in play. The load-bearing hazard is decimal place value — the 'add/remove a zero' shortcut fails (3250 g ÷ 1000 is 3.25 kg, not 325), and children who think 'the point is the decimal' misplace digits.
bestPractices: Convert by moving the DIGITS across a fixed decimal point (×/÷ by 10/100/1000), explicitly rejecting 'add a zero' and 'move the point' — use true/false error-spotting (0.45÷10 = .45?) to confront the shortcut (NCETM Spine 2.29).
Keep the unit-size reasoning from Year 5 ('larger unit → fewer → divide') so direction is reasoned, not guessed.
Make the powers-of-10 STRUCTURE explicit: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1000 m = 1 km — so a conversion is one multiplication/division by a power of ten, and mixed chains compose.
Use a place-value chart extended to thousandths so pupils can state the value of each digit before and after, and place holder zeros correctly.
Include a reasonableness check (should the number get bigger or smaller?) to catch direction and decimal-placement errors.

commonMisconceptions: 'Add/remove a zero' with decimals: 3250 g → '325 kg', or 0.45 km → '45 m' / '4.5 m'.
Reverses the multiply/divide direction, giving an answer orders of magnitude out (0.45 km → 0.00045 m).
'The point is the decimal' — mis-values digits after the point or treats 0.45 as the whole number 45.
Cannot articulate the powers-of-10 relationship, so treats each conversion as an isolated fact.

learn.summary: Year 6 pupils (age 10–11) convert between standard measurement units using decimal notation to up to three decimal places, moving in both directions (smaller↔larger), and explain the mm–cm–m–km (and g–kg, ml–l) relationships as powers of ten. This extends Year 5 conversion with the decimal point now in play: the method stays 'reason from unit size, then move the DIGITS across a fixed decimal point', using ×/÷ by 10/100/1000. The load-bearing hazard is decimal place value — the 'add/remove a zero' shortcut fails (3250 g ÷ 1000 = 3.25 kg, not 325), and children who think 'the point is the decimal fraction' misplace digit values.

activities.title: Move the digits, keep the point still (place-value conversion)
feedback: If a learner answers 325 kg for 3250 g, they removed zeros instead of moving digits three places. Rebuild it on the chart: 3250 ÷ 1000 moves each digit three places right, giving 3.25 — count the places, do not delete symbols.

If a learner answers 4.5 m or 45 m for 0.45 km, name the error precisely: 4.5 m is a one-place shift (as if ×10), and 45 m is a two-place shift (as if ×100). Both are wrong; 0.45 × 1000 moves digits three places left to 450 m. Have them name the value of the 4 (four tenths) and the 5 (five hundredths) first, then shift three places.
If an answer is wildly out (e.g. 0.00045 m or 3 250 000 kg), the multiply/divide direction was reversed. Re-reason from unit size before trusting the result.
If a learner treats 0.45 as the whole number 45, rebuild decimal place value: each column to the right is ten times smaller, so 0.45 is four tenths and five hundredths.
activities.rationale: Converting by moving digits across a fixed point directly confronts the 'add/remove a zero' shortcut, which fails for decimals; pairing it with explicit unit-size reasoning keeps direction reasoned rather than guessed, and the equal-value check (3.250 = 3.25) addresses holder-zero confusion. The 5 cm→0.05 m case instances the same method on a shorter chain.

learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart extended to thousandths. Write 3250 g in it, then convert to kilograms by sliding every digit three places to the RIGHT (dividing by 1000) while the decimal point stays fixed, landing on 3.25 kg; note that a holder zero is inserted only where place value demands it.
Before moving, state the unit-size reason aloud: 'Kilograms are the bigger unit, so there will be FEWER of them — I divide.' Then check the direction of the digit shift matches.
Convert the reverse case 0.45 km to metres (×1000), sliding digits three places LEFT to get 450 m; state that metres are smaller, so there are MORE.

Convert 5 cm to 0.05 m (÷100), sliding each digit two places to the right — a shorter example of the same digit-movement method with decimal notation; say why metres are the larger unit so there are fewer.
Confirm that 3.250 kg and 3.25 kg name the same quantity — the trailing zero after the last significant digit does not change the value.
Do a reasonableness check each time: 'Should this number get bigger or smaller?' and reject any answer that is orders of magnitude out.
activities.intendedInsight: A conversion moves the SAME digits across a FIXED decimal point; the point does not move. Converting to a larger unit gives fewer of them (divide, digits move right); converting to a smaller unit gives more (multiply, digits move left). 3250 g and 3.25 kg are one quantity; 3.250 equals 3.25.

activities.title: Spot the false shortcut (error-spotting with decimals)
feedback: If a learner accepts 0.45 ÷ 10 = .45, show on the chart that dividing by ten moves each digit one place right: 0.45 → 0.045. Nothing was divided in '.45'.
If a learner accepts 25.34 × 10 = 25.340, point out that 25.340 equals 25.34 (same value). Multiplying by ten gives 253.4 — digits move one place left.
activities.rationale: True/false error-spotting on carefully chosen decimal cases makes the failure of the zero shortcut explicit and forces articulation of digit movement and place value.
sourceClaims: Convert measures by moving the DIGITS across a fixed decimal point via ×/÷ by 10/100/1000; the guide embeds 'add/remove a zero' as FALSE statements for decimals (0.45÷10 = .45; 25.34×10 = 25.340) to expose the misconception.
A common decimal misconception is thinking 'the point is the decimal fraction'; place value must extend so each column to the right is ten times smaller, and holder zeros are understood.
learnerActions: Judge true or false and explain: 'Is 0.45 ÷ 10 = .45?' Correct it to 0.045 by moving each digit one place right.
Judge true or false: 'Is 25.34 × 10 = 25.340?' Explain that appending a zero after the last decimal does NOT multiply by ten; the correct answer is 253.4, with digits moving one place left.
For each false statement, state the correct conversion and justify it with the value of each digit and the direction of movement.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or removing a zero is not the same as multiplying or dividing by a power of ten once decimals are involved. ×/÷ by 10, 100, 1000 moves the digits by one, two, or three places; the zero trick coincidentally works for some whole numbers but misvalues decimals.

activities.title: Climb the powers-of-ten ladder (composing conversions)
feedback: If a learner cannot say why 1 km = 1000 m, walk the ladder rung by rung (m → ×10 → tens of metres → ×10 → hundreds → ×10 → 1000 m) so the ×1000 is seen as 10×10×10.
If a learner treats g–kg differently from m–km, point out both are ÷1000 (or ×1000) — the same power-of-ten structure applies.
activities.rationale: Making the powers-of-ten structure explicit lets conversions be reasoned and composed rather than memorised, which supports transfer across length, mass and volume.
sourceClaims: UK DfE Year 6 pupils solve problems involving conversion of units using decimal notation up to three decimal places, converting length/mass/volume/time from a smaller unit to a larger and vice versa.
A common decimal misconception is thinking 'the point is the decimal fraction'; place value must extend so each column to the right is ten times smaller, and holder zeros are understood.
learnerActions: Build a ladder stating each relationship: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1000 m = 1 km. For each rung, say whether you multiply or divide and by what power of ten.
Hop along the ladder to compose a chain, e.g. mm → cm (÷10) → m (÷100) → km (÷1000), and recognise that any single conversion is one multiplication or division by a power of ten.
Optionally use a Gattegno chart (rows for powers of ten) to see each conversion as a single ×/÷ by a power of ten — moving along a row, or jumping rows for the larger steps.
Explain in words why 1 km is a thousand metres and not a hundred, using the powers-of-ten structure rather than reciting it as an isolated fact.

Transfer the same structure to mass (g–kg) and volume (ml–l) to show the method is general across metric units, not tied to length. Then contrast with time (e.g. 2.5 h = 150 min, not 250 min) to see that time units use factors of 60 and 24, not powers of ten.
activities.intendedInsight: The metric system is built on powers of ten, so every metric conversion is a single ×/÷ by a power of ten and mixed chains compose; knowing the structure removes the need to memorise each conversion separately. Time units are not decimal (60 s = 1 min, 60 min = 1 h, 24 h = 1 day), so time conversions use those factors instead of powers of ten.

constraints: Reject 'add/remove a zero' and 'move the decimal point' as methods; teach movement of the DIGITS across a point that stays fixed.
Keep unit-size reasoning ('larger unit → fewer → divide; smaller unit → more → multiply') so direction is reasoned, not guessed, and pair it with a reasonableness check.

A fixed reference ladder of powers of ten can show the relationships but does not let a learner move digits or check direction themselves; use it alongside an activity where the learner performs the transformation (chart, writing, or spoken step-by-step), not as the only medium.

Matching, fill-in-the-blank and multiple-choice items (including true/false decimal cases) can probe direction and the add-a-zero error precisely, but recognition responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the conversion; include tasks where the learner produces the converted value and justifies it.
Ensure a holder zero is inserted only where place value requires it (e.g. 0.045), and that trailing zeros after the last significant decimal (3.250 vs 3.25) are recognised as equal value.

An extended place-value chart to thousandths, a double number line between the two units, and a Gattegno chart for ×/÷ by powers of ten are useful supports but are scaffolds; learners should also reason and state values without them to show secure understanding.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3250 g ÷ 1000 = 3.25 kg (digits move three places right); 0.45 km × 1000 = 450 m (three places left); 5 cm ÷ 100 = 0.05 m (two places right); 0.45 ÷ 10 = 0.045 (one place right); 25.34 × 10 = 253.4 (one place left, NOT 25.340). All checked and consistent with the source's intended corrections. The misconception answers (325 kg, 45 m, 4.5 m, 25.340, 0.00045 m, 3 250 000 kg) appear only as errors to correct, never as valid answers.

The original source frames an interactive place-value slider as 'ideal' and a static image/3D/dialogue as 'poor' for this topic. These are catalog fit rankings, not established comparative efficacy; this rewrite retains the digit-movement mechanism as a concrete support while softening claims that other media 'cannot teach' the concept. A static ladder, Gattegno chart, and spoken/written reasoning can also support the objective.
The Gattegno chart from the original keyRepresentations is retained as an optional scaffold in the powers-of-ten activity and the scaffold constraint.
One listed source (DfE National Curriculum) carries verified:false in the row; treat its claim with appropriate caution pending verification.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Add/remove a zero' with decimals — divides 3250 by 1000 by deleting zeros ('325 kg'), or multiplies 0.45 by 1000 by appending/one-step zeros ('45 m' or '4.5 m').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Move digits three places on a place-value chart with the point fixed; use true/false items (0.45÷10 = .45? 25.34×10 = 25.340?) to show the zero shortcut fails for decimals.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The answer has the wrong number of decimal places; zeros were added/removed rather than digits moved three places.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the multiply/divide direction — gives an answer orders of magnitude out (0.45 km → 0.00045 m, or 3250 g → 3 250 000 kg).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reason from unit size first ('metres smaller → more → multiply') and add a reasonableness check before trusting the answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The result is far bigger/smaller than sensible; no unit-size reasoning offered.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The point is the decimal' — mis-values digits after the point, treating 0.45 as the whole number 45 or misreading thousandths.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild decimal place value: each column right is ten times smaller; state the value of each digit in 0.45 (four tenths, five hundredths) before converting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Digit values after the point are wrong; 0.45 handled as 45; three-decimal-place answers misplaced.

responseLevels.gap: Adds/removes zeros, reverses direction, or mis-values decimal digits; answers orders of magnitude out.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions with correct decimal placement (digits move, point fixed), handles up to 3 dp, and explains the ×/÷ powers-of-10 structure linking mm–cm–m–km — transferring across length, mass, volume and time.
responseLevels.partial: Converts a friendly case correctly but slips on three decimal places or on the reverse direction, or converts but cannot explain the powers-of-10 relationship.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to think aloud through three tasks: (1) 'Convert 3250 g to kilograms.' (2) 'Convert 0.45 km to metres.' (3) 'Explain how mm, cm, m and km are related using powers of 10.' Watch the direction choice, where the decimal point ends up, and whether the powers-of-10 structure is understood — not just the final numbers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil with secure decimal place value moves the digits the right number of places in the right direction (3.25 kg; 450 m) and explains the ×10 chain; a pupil relying on 'add/remove a zero' produces 325 kg or 45 m, and one who thinks 'the point is the decimal' mis-values 0.45. Digit-movement understanding versus zero-shortcut diverge precisely on these decimal cases.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Measurement Conversions
topic.description: Solve problems involving the calculation and conversion of units of measure, using decimal notation and multi-step reasoning in real-world contexts
evidence: Solve: 'A recipe uses 0.75 kg of flour. How many grams are needed for 3 batches?'
Compare 2.5 litres and 2,450 ml by converting to the same unit
Solve a multi-step problem involving time, distance, and unit conversion
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is filling a fish tank that holds 60 litres and the tap fills it at 3.5 litres per minute, can they work out how long it will take to fill the tank?

pedagogy.summary: Year 6 (age 10–11) pupils solve MULTI-STEP real-world problems that require converting units and then calculating (or comparing) — e.g. scaling a recipe given in kilograms into grams across several batches, or comparing 2.5 l with 2450 ml. The new demand over pure conversion is SEQUENCING: decide when to convert, put quantities into a common unit before comparing or operating, and check the result is reasonable. It rests on secure decimal conversion (Y6) and on word-problem modelling; the classic failures are comparing raw numbers without converting, and dropping or reversing the conversion step inside a longer chain.
bestPractices: Insist on a COMMON unit before comparing or combining — convert 2.5 l to 2500 ml (or 2450 ml to 2.45 l) first; never compare '2450 vs 2.5'.
Model the problem structure (bar model / double number line) and plan the steps: which quantities to convert, in which direction, then which operation.
Keep the unit-size reasoning and digit-movement conversion from earlier years, and label units at every step so a stray 'g' vs 'kg' is caught.
Estimate first and sense-check the final answer's size and unit (2250 g is sensible for 3 batches; 2250 kg is not).
Vary contexts (mass, capacity, length, time, money) and step order (convert-then-operate vs operate-then-convert) so the method generalises.
keyRepresentations: Bar model / double number line for the multi-step structure
Common-unit number line for comparisons
Place-value chart for the embedded conversion step
Labelled step-by-step working (unit tracked at each line)
commonMisconceptions: Compares measurements without converting to a common unit ('2450 ml > 2.5 l because 2450 > 2.5').
Drops the conversion step or reverses its direction inside a multi-step chain (0.75 × 3 = 2.25 reported as '2.25 g').
Loses track across steps or never estimates, so an unreasonable answer (2250 kg of flour) passes unnoticed.
Treats a mixed/decimal measure as two separate whole numbers when operating.

learn.summary: Year 6 pupils (age 10–11) solve multi-step, real-world measurement problems that require unit conversion plus calculation or comparison — e.g. scaling a 0.75 kg recipe across 3 batches, or deciding whether 2.5 litres or 2450 ml is more. The new demand beyond pure conversion is SEQUENCING: deciding when and in which direction to convert, putting quantities into a common unit before comparing or operating, labelling units at every step, and sense-checking the final answer's size and unit against an estimate. Classic failures are comparing raw numbers without converting, dropping or reversing the conversion inside a longer chain, treating a decimal measure as two separate whole numbers, and accepting an unreasonable answer unchecked.

activities.title: Recipe scaler: convert, operate, and track the unit
feedback: If a learner writes '2.25 g', prompt: '2.25 what? You multiplied kilograms — is 2.25 g sensible for three batches of flour, or did the kg→g conversion get dropped?'
If the answer comes out as 2250 kg, prompt: 'Roughly how much flour did you expect for 3 batches? Does 2250 kg fit that estimate?'
If a learner converts the wrong way (e.g. 0.75 kg → 0.00075 g), ask them to reason about unit size: grams are smaller than kilograms, so the number of grams should be larger, not smaller.

If a learner treats 2.25 as the separate whole numbers '2' and '25', remind them a decimal measure is one quantity, not two: in 2.25 kg the '.25' means 0.25 kg, which is 250 g (NOT a separate '25'), so 2.25 kg = 2250 g — the digits after the point are not a second whole number.
Reinforce correct work: 'You labelled the unit on each line, so a stray g vs kg would have been caught — that is exactly the habit that guards multi-step answers.'
activities.rationale: Year 6 curricula require solving problems involving the calculation AND conversion of units of measure with decimal notation; embedding a ×/÷ by 10/100/1000 conversion inside a longer chain is where drop-a-step and direction errors appear, and estimating first gives a sense of a reasonable answer so errors are detected.
sourceClaims: Grade 5 pupils use unit conversions in solving multi-step, real-world problems (5.MD.A.1 explicitly names multi-step real-world problem solving).
Convert measures via ×/÷ by 10/100/1000 (digits move, point fixed); this conversion skill is what a multi-step problem embeds, and direction errors follow from not reasoning about unit size.
Pupils rarely estimate before calculating and so lack a sense of a reasonable answer, leaving multi-step errors undetected.
UK DfE Year 6 pupils solve problems involving the calculation and conversion of units of measure, using decimal notation up to three decimal places where appropriate.
learnerActions: Take the problem 'A recipe uses 0.75 kg of flour — how many grams are needed for 3 batches?' and FIRST write a rough estimate of the expected answer (about 2 to 2.5 kg, i.e. roughly 2000–2500 g).
Plan the steps on a bar model or double number line: decide which quantity needs converting and in which direction (0.75 kg → 750 g), then which operation (×3).
Execute either order — convert then operate (0.75 kg → 750 g, ×3 = 2250 g) or operate then convert (0.75 × 3 = 2.25 kg = 2250 g) — writing the unit on every line of working.
Compare the final answer to your up-front estimate: check both the size and the unit (2250 g is sensible for 3 batches; 2250 kg or '2.25 g' is not).

Repeat with a different context and step order (e.g. mass, capacity, length, time, money) so the method generalises, remembering that time conversions use 60 (minutes/seconds) or 24 (hours/days) rather than 10, 100 or 1000 (e.g. 1.5 hours = 90 minutes, not 150).
activities.intendedInsight: A multi-step measurement answer is only trustworthy when each quantity is converted correctly, the unit is carried through every step, and the final size and unit match a sensible up-front estimate.

activities.title: Which is more? Compare on a common-unit number line
feedback: If a learner decides 2450 ml > 2.5 l 'because 2450 > 2.5', ask: 'Are those in the same unit yet? Make them match first, then decide.'
After a correct conversion, confirm: 'Now both are in millilitres — 2500 vs 2450 — so the comparison is fair and 2.5 l is more.'
Challenge with a pair where the bigger number is the smaller amount, so that converting first becomes essential rather than optional.
activities.rationale: Children commonly treat measurements as separate whole numbers and compare on the digits without a common unit; competence with two-place amounts does not guarantee correct handling across units, so forcing a common unit before deciding targets the misconception directly.
sourceClaims: Children treat measurements as separate whole numbers and compare/operate on the digits without putting them in a common unit; competence with two-place amounts does not guarantee correct handling across units.
learnerActions: Take two measurements in different units — 2.5 litres and 2450 ml — and notice they cannot be judged directly because '2.5' and '2450' are not in the same unit.
Convert one to match the other (2.5 l → 2500 ml, or 2450 ml → 2.45 l), stating which unit you chose and why.
Place both converted values on a single common-unit number line and read off which is larger (2500 ml clearly overtakes 2450 ml).
State the comparison in words: 'you can only compare like with like,' then explain which original measurement was more.
Try further pairs across mass, capacity and length where the raw digits are misleading (e.g. the amount with the bigger bare number is actually smaller).
activities.intendedInsight: Two measurements cannot be compared or combined until they are expressed in the same unit; the bare digits can be misleading, so convert to a common unit first.

activities.title: Order the solution steps
feedback: If steps are ordered so the conversion is omitted, point to the resulting mis-unit answer and ask the learner to reinsert the missing conversion.
Praise an ordering that converts to a common unit before comparing or operating, noting this is the habit that keeps the unit correct through the chain.
activities.rationale: Solving multi-step real-world problems requires correct sequencing of conversion and operation steps; an ordering task is proposed as a way to make that structure explicit and to surface the drop-a-step error, and planning the structure (bar model / double number line) may reduce working-memory load so steps are monitored rather than lost. Such a task can both rehearse and reveal sequencing, not only grade it.
sourceClaims: Grade 5 pupils use unit conversions in solving multi-step, real-world problems (5.MD.A.1 explicitly names multi-step real-world problem solving).
learnerActions: For a multi-step problem (e.g. time, distance and unit conversion combined), lay out the solution stages as cards or lines and put them in the correct order BEFORE computing; note that any time conversion uses 60 or 24, not a power of 10.
Decide explicitly where the conversion belongs in the sequence and which direction it goes, then fill in each conversion and operation.
After solving, justify why that order works: say which quantity ends up larger or which operation must come next and why.
Mark where a 'drop-a-step' error would occur if the conversion were skipped, and show what wrong answer it would produce.
activities.intendedInsight: Multi-step problems succeed or fail on the ORDER and completeness of steps; naming where the conversion sits in the chain helps prevent dropping or reversing it.

constraints: Always require a COMMON unit before comparing or combining; never let a learner compare '2450 vs 2.5' as bare numbers.

Label the unit at every line of working so a stray 'g' vs 'kg' is caught, and keep the unit-size reasoning from earlier years; digit-movement (×/÷ 10, 100, 1000) only works for metric conversions and money (£ to p), not time, which uses 60 and 24.
Estimate first and sense-check the final answer's size AND unit before accepting it.
Vary contexts (mass, capacity, length, time, money) and both step orders (convert-then-operate and operate-then-convert) so the method generalises rather than being tied to one worked example.

Recognition-only or multiple-choice checks can confirm which is more after conversion but do not by themselves elicit the independent planning and step-tracking; pair them with constructed working where the learner writes and labels each step.

A static worked example can show the method but cannot give per-step feedback or let the learner commit a conversion and get it flagged; treat any fixed picture as a reference, not the main vehicle for practising sequencing.
Spatial/3D representation adds little for this particular task since the reasoning here is numeric and sequential; bar models and number lines carry the structure for these problems.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 0.75 kg = 750 g; 750 × 3 = 2250 g; equivalently 0.75 × 3 = 2.25 kg = 2250 g — consistent, so a rough estimate of about 2–2.5 kg brackets the answer. 2.5 l = 2500 ml > 2450 ml — correct. The deliberately wrong learner outputs ('2.25 g', 2250 kg, 0.00075 g) are flagged as errors in feedback, not presented as valid answers. Note 0.25 kg = 250 g (clarified in Activity 1 feedback to avoid reinforcing a '25 g' misread).

The source notes two citations (NCETM 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives' and the DfE National Curriculum) carry verified:false in the original row; their supporting claims are retained but their verification status is unconfirmed here.

Original guidance framed a static image as unable to 'support sequencing' and a conversation as unable to 'drive multi-step calculation'; these were softened to scoped affordance/limit statements, since catalog fit ratings do not establish universal necessity.

Activity 3's claim that the ordering task is diagnostic of the drop-a-step error and reduces working-memory load is a design proposal; the retained CCSS source claim establishes the multi-step problem-solving context but does not itself verify that diagnostic/load benefit.

Editorial changes on review: Activity 1 feedback on reading a decimal as two whole numbers was clarified so the correction explicitly states 0.25 kg = 250 g (not 25 g); earlier edits had raised the Activity 1 estimate band to about 2–2.5 kg so it brackets 2250 g and removed the 'rarely estimate' claim from the ordering activity.

'Your answer is 2.25 — 2.25 what? Is that grams or kilograms, and is that sensible for three batches?'
'Roughly how much flour did you expect for 3 batches? Does your exact answer fit that?'
'Show me the order of your steps — where did you convert, and why there?'

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is driving 40 miles to a theme park, can they use the rule that 5 miles ≈ 8 km to estimate roughly how many kilometres that is?

pedagogy.summary: Children convert between miles and kilometres using the approximate relationship 5 miles ≈ 8 km (equivalently ≈ ×1.6). The heart of the topic is proportional (multiplicative) reasoning: converting is scaling the ratio 5:8 up or down, not adding a constant. Key facts to establish are that one mile is a GREATER distance than one kilometre (so a distance is a bigger number in km than in miles), that ≈ means 'approximately equal to', and that the relationship is a direct proportion whose conversion graph is a straight line through the origin. The double number line, ratio table and conversion graph are three views of the same multiplicative structure, and comparing UK distances (miles) with European ones (km) gives authentic context.
bestPractices: Establish the ratio 5 miles ≈ 8 km and read it both ways; teach ≈ explicitly and expect 'about' answers.
Represent with a double number line and ratio table so children SCALE the ratio (5:8 → 15:24) multiplicatively, and explicitly contrast this with the wrong additive strategy.
Use a 'spot the mistake' task where a character adds or subtracts the same amount to both quantities, and have children explain why it is wrong.
Make the 'which unit is larger' point concrete: a mile is longer, so any distance is a bigger number of km than of miles; use this to sense-check the direction of a conversion.
Connect the conversion to its straight-line graph through the origin as preparation for proportional graphs, and to real comparisons (a 10 km race vs a 6-mile run).
keyRepresentations: Double number line (miles and km aligned from 0)
Ratio / conversion table
Conversion graph (straight line through the origin, gradient ≈ 1.6)
'Spot the mistake' worked example exposing additive error
commonMisconceptions: Additive rather than multiplicative reasoning ('two more miles means two more km'; from 10 miles ≈ 16 km, adds 5 to both to convert 15 miles).
Thinks a kilometre is longer than a mile because the same distance is a bigger number in km, so converts in the wrong direction.
Treats 5 miles = 8 km as exact rather than approximate, ignoring ≈.

activities.title: Slide and scale: the conversion stays on one straight line

If a learner divides or gives fewer km than miles (~9 km), remind them a mile is the longer unit: 5 miles needs 8 km to cover the same distance, so any distance is a bigger number of km than of miles.
Reinforce that each answer is 'about': ≈ means approximately, so 24 km is a sensible estimate (true value ~24.14 km), not exact.
activities.rationale: Aligning a double number line, ratio table and conversion graph makes the multiplicative structure one coherent picture and prepares children for proportional graphs; an optional live/draggable version lets children watch scaled points stay on the origin ray while additive points drift further away from it (repeatedly adding the same amount to both gives points on a different straight line, with gradient 1, that does not pass through the origin). A 'spot the mistake' contrast targets the documented additive error.

'Children need to know that one mile is a greater distance than one kilometre… 5 miles is approximately equal to 8 km.' Misconceptions verbatim: children may think a kilometre is longer than a mile since the same distance is a greater number in km (15 miles ≈ 24 km); and may use additive rather than multiplicative reasoning (10 miles ≈ 16 km, so add 5 to both for 15 miles).

'If five miles is equivalent to eight kilometres, how many kilometres is seven miles? Students may respond that two more miles means two more kilometres.' Students should see multiplication as scaling, not repeated addition; a proportional relationship y = kx plots as a straight line through the origin; scalar (along the line) vs functional (between the lines, ×1.6) multipliers.
learnerActions: Work with a double number line AND a matching ratio table, both with miles and km aligned from 0, showing the pairs 5↔8, 10↔16, 15↔24.

Scale the ratio up and down multiplicatively: state that 15 miles is 3 lots of 5 miles, so it is 3 lots of 8 km = 24 km; extend to 40 miles ≈ 64 km (×8), and confirm the ×1.6 'between the lines' multiplier.

Connect the pairs to a conversion graph: plot the pairs and confirm they lie on one straight line through the origin (with miles on the horizontal axis and km on the vertical axis, the gradient is about 1.6).

Then try a character's 'add 5 to both' shortcut (5 miles, 8 km → 10 miles, 13 km) and plot that point; notice it falls OFF the origin line (the true pair is 10 miles ↔ 16 km) and explain why the shortcut is wrong.
Use a compare task: place a 10 km race and a 6-mile run (≈ 9.6 km) on the same line and decide which reaches further (the 10 km race).
activities.intendedInsight: Converting means scaling the ratio 5:8 (multiplying), which keeps every point on the same straight line through zero; adding a constant to both quantities knocks points off that line and is wrong.

activities.title: Spot the mistake: additive versus multiplicative conversion
feedback: For the '23 km' example: adding 15 to both does not preserve the 5:8 ratio; scale instead — 20 miles is 4 lots of 5 miles, so 4 lots of 8 km = 32 km.
If ~18 km is chosen: this comes from starting at 5 mi ≈ 8 km and adding ~1 km per extra mile; triple the whole ratio instead (8 → 24 km for 15 miles).
If ~9 km is chosen: this divides and treats a km as the larger unit; a mile is longer, so the km figure must be larger than the mile figure (about 24 km).
activities.rationale: A dedicated 'spot the mistake' task where a character adds or subtracts the same amount to both quantities, with children explaining why it is wrong, is a recommended way to expose the additive misconception. Conversion and comparison items with documented distractors can check whether reasoning is multiplicative, though a selection item alone does not build graph intuition and should be paired with building pairs on a number line, ratio table or graph.

learnerActions: Read a character's converted answer and decide if it is right, e.g. '5 miles ≈ 8 km, so 20 miles ≈ 8 + 15 = 23 km'.
Identify the wrong strategy (adding a constant to both quantities) and compute the correct answer multiplicatively (20 miles = 4 × 5 miles = 4 × 8 km = 32 km).
Convert 15 miles and choose among sensible and faulty options, explaining why the additive (~18 km) and wrong-direction (~9 km) options are wrong.
Explain the error in words: why does adding the same amount to both quantities break the proportion?
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising and articulating the additive error consolidates that conversion scales the ratio; the characteristic wrong answers (~18 km additive, ~9 km wrong-direction) typically come from misreading the proportional structure or the direction of conversion rather than from arithmetic slips.

constraints: Treat the relationship as approximate throughout: teach ≈ explicitly and expect 'about' answers; 5 miles ≈ 8 km (true value for 15 miles is ~24.14 km), never exact.

A static aligned double number line with tap-to-reveal pairs conveys the fact pairs but cannot show the additive error in motion; it can still display a plotted additive point statically. Use it as a scaffold and make the multiplicative/additive contrast explicit.

A single selection-based spot-the-mistake item can assess whether reasoning is multiplicative but does not by itself build graph intuition; pair it with construction of pairs on a number line, ratio table or graph.
Keep the direction check concrete: a mile is longer, so the km figure for a given distance is always the bigger number — use this to sense-check every conversion.

topic.name: Measuring & Plotting Lengths
topic.description: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths to the nearest whole unit and display the data on a line plot
evidence: Measure the lengths of several objects and record the data
Create a line plot with a horizontal scale marked in whole-number units
Interpret a line plot to answer questions about the data
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures the length of ten leaves to the nearest cm and records the results, can they display the data on a simple number-line plot — grouping leaves of the same length?

pedagogy.summary: Children measure several real objects to the nearest whole unit and display them on a line plot: a horizontal number line marked in equal whole-number intervals with one X stacked above each measured value. The line plot is where measuring, counting and the number line meet — the horizontal axis is a true measurement scale (equal intervals, every value shown even when no data lands there), height tells you HOW MANY objects, position tells you HOW LONG. The procedure is best taught by having children generate their OWN data, then build the plot on a pre-scaled line, keeping the ruler physically aligned under the axis so 'position = length' is felt, not just told.
bestPractices: Have children measure real objects they care about and record the data first, then plot — the plot should display data they generated
Provide a pre-drawn horizontal line and stress that the scale is a ruler: equal intervals, every whole-number value present even if no X sits above it
Keep an actual ruler aligned beneath the plot so the X's position reads as a length on the same scale
Explicitly separate the two questions the plot answers: 'how many?' (count the Xs) versus 'how long?' (read the position)
Bridge from earlier tally/categorical work but flag the key shift — the axis is now a measurement scale, not arbitrary categories
keyRepresentations: The horizontal number line as a measurement scale (equal whole-unit intervals)
Stacked X marks, one X per object
A ruler aligned under the plot linking measured length to axis position
A tally / frequency table as a bridge from raw measurements to the plot
commonMisconceptions: Reading the height of a stack as the length ('the tallest stack is the longest object')
Drawing only the values that occurred and spacing them evenly, so a value with no data is omitted and the intervals become unequal
Measuring from the 1 mark or the ruler's end instead of zero, so every length is off by a unit
Treating each X as one unit of length rather than one object

learn.summary: Children generate their own measurement data by measuring several real objects to the nearest whole unit, then display the data on a line plot: a horizontal number line marked in equal whole-number intervals with one X stacked above each measured value. The horizontal axis is a true measurement scale (equal intervals, every value shown even when no data lands there); height tells you HOW MANY objects, position tells you HOW LONG. Teaching works best when children measure first, then build the plot, with a ruler kept physically aligned under the axis so 'position = length' is felt. A line may be pre-scaled as an early scaffold, but constructing the scale on a plain line is the fuller skill the objective targets. A tally or frequency table can bridge from raw measurements, but the axis is an ordered measurement scale, not the reorderable categories of earlier tally/category charts. Core activity: a measure-and-plot build (hands-on or on-screen). Supporting activities: interpreting a given plot, and a reference/reveal of a finished plot for the meaning of each X and position.

activities.title: Measure your own objects, then build the line plot
feedback: If a child reads a tall stack as a long object, slide the real ruler under the plot and ask them to point to where an object of that length would actually sit; hold the two questions apart — 'how many objects?' versus 'how long is one?'

If a child treats each X as a unit of length (e.g. 'three Xs means 3 cm long'), clarify that each X stands for one object placed at its measured position; the length is read from the horizontal scale, not from how many Xs are stacked.

If a child leaves out a value nothing measured (e.g. axis reads 3,4,6,7 with 5 missing), reteach the axis as a ruler — every unit is present whether or not data lands on it; overlay a real ruler and mark the empty value together.

If a child reorders or evenly spaces only the values that occurred (as in a category chart), remind them the axis is an ordered measurement scale where position means length, so every unit must appear in order.
If every measurement is off by one unit, pause the plotting and reteach measuring from zero with gap-free unit iteration before returning.

When a child notices a whole-number value on the scale with no X above it, confirm that the empty spot is meaningful: it shows no object had that length, and the scale keeps it open. If a child has put an X at a value nothing measured, have them check their recorded data and remove it.
If a second object also measures 6, confirm its X stacks above the first at the same position — the stack grows upward (count) while the position stays fixed (length).
activities.rationale: The standard describes a procedure — generate measurement data, then show it on a line plot with a horizontal whole-number scale — so children should actually measure and build rather than only read. Learners who carry over bar/case-value habits confuse stack height (frequency) with the variable value (position); pairing the ruler with the axis targets that specific confusion.
sourceClaims: Grade 2 standard: generate measurement data by measuring lengths of several objects to the nearest whole unit; show the measurements by making a line plot with a horizontal scale marked off in whole-number units.

Students familiar with bar / case-value graphs transfer the habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (y-axis / stack height) with the value of the variable (x-axis / position); even after instruction nearly 20% report the frequency at the centre rather than the variable value, and this axis confusion appears in simple dot plots too.
learnerActions: Collect 6-8 small real objects (pencils, crayons, leaves, blocks) and measure each to the nearest whole centimetre, measuring from the ruler's zero mark, not from 1 or the end.
Record each measurement in a simple tally or frequency table as a bridge from raw measurements to the plot.

Notice how a line plot differs from earlier tally or category charts: here the horizontal axis is an ordered measurement scale with equal whole-number intervals and every value present, not a set of arbitrary categories you could reorder or leave out.

On a horizontal line, mark the scale as equal whole-number intervals across the full range of your data, including any whole-number value that nothing measured. Early on a line that is already pre-scaled can be provided as a scaffold so you focus on plotting; building the scale yourself afterwards is the fuller skill this topic is aiming at.
Place exactly one X above each object's measured value; when two objects share a length, stack a second X on top of the first.

If your scale marks are spaced 1 cm apart, keep an actual ruler aligned directly beneath the line, with its numbers matching your scale labels, so each X's horizontal position reads as a length on the same scale.
Answer two separate questions from your finished plot: 'How many objects were 6 cm?' (count the Xs in that stack) and 'How long is the longest object?' (read its position on the scale).
activities.intendedInsight: On a line plot the sideways position of an X answers 'how long?' while the upward height of a stack answers 'how many?'. Unlike reorderable categorical charts, the axis is a ruler-like measurement scale: equal intervals with every whole-number value staying on it even when no object landed there, so the gaps stay equal.

activities.title: Interpret a given line plot: how many versus how long
feedback: If a child answers 'how long is the longest?' with a stack's count, redirect them to the horizontal scale and ask them to read the position of the rightmost X.
If a child ignores an empty scale value, ask what it tells them about objects of that length.
Confirm that adding an object changes the count of a stack but not the positions already on the plot.
activities.rationale: Interpreting a given plot isolates the value-versus-frequency distinction that learners commonly collapse. This supports but does not replace the generative build, since reading a finished plot does not require constructing the scale or measuring.
sourceClaims: Students familiar with bar / case-value graphs transfer the habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (y-axis / stack height) with the value of the variable (x-axis / position); even after instruction nearly 20% report the frequency at the centre rather than the variable value, and this axis confusion appears in simple dot plots too.
learnerActions: Study a completed line plot and answer count questions such as 'How many objects were 6 cm long?' by counting the Xs in a stack.
Answer position questions such as 'How long is the longest object?' by reading the scale, not the stack height.
Explain what an empty whole-number value on the scale means (no object had that length).
Predict what changes if one more object measuring 6 cm were added (one more X on the 6 stack; the position is unchanged).
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a line plot means deliberately choosing between counting (height) and reading position (length); the same plot answers both kinds of question in different ways.

activities.title: Reference reveal: what each X and each position means
feedback: If a child confuses the two, pair each reveal with the question it answers ('how many' at a stack, 'how long' at a position).
Note that this reference shows meaning but does not by itself let a child generate data or feel the measure-then-plot link.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal or point-and-name reference clarifies the meaning of marks and positions and can scaffold self-checking. It is a reference, not a substitute for building the plot from one's own measurements.
learnerActions: Point to (or tap) a stack and state 'how many' objects it represents.
Point to (or tap) a position on the scale and state 'how long' that is.
Use the finished plot as a reference while checking a plot you built yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: Each X stands for one object, placed at its measured length; a stack's height is a count, its position is a length.

constraints: The core objective is a procedure: children must actually measure objects and construct the scale and marks, not only read or recognise a finished plot. A pre-scaled line is an acceptable early scaffold, but children should reach the point of building the scale themselves.
Children should generate and record their own data before plotting, so the plot displays data they produced.

The horizontal axis must be an ordered measurement scale: equal whole-unit intervals across the full range, with every whole-number value present even where no data lands — unlike reorderable categorical/tally charts.

Measure from zero with gap-free unit iteration; measuring from the 1 mark makes every length one unit too long, and measuring from the ruler's physical end can make lengths wrong by the size of any gap before the zero mark.
One X per object; two equal-length objects produce a stack of two at the same position. Each X represents an object, not a unit of length.

Interpreting a given plot and reveal-the-meaning references are supporting scaffolds: they can assess or clarify interpretation but do not exercise the generative measure-and-scale skill, so do not rely on them alone.
Keeping a real ruler aligned under the axis is a concrete device to link length to position; it is one effective option, not the only way to teach the link.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row asserts that a static picture or a quiz 'cannot teach' the position-from-height separation and empty-value requirement. This comparative-necessity claim is not established by the cited sources; it has been softened to scope each format's affordances and limits. A fixed/reveal reference or an interpretation quiz can still support learning, though neither elicits independent construction of the scale.

The original marked 3D and conversation formats as 'poor' with claims like '3D adds nothing' and 'dialogue has no purchase'; these universal claims are not supported by the sources and have been omitted rather than propagated. The planar nature of a line plot is noted as a reason 2D construction fits the task without asserting other media teach nothing.

The original is internally mixed on whether the line is pre-scaled (its pedagogy best practice) or plain/unmarked for the child to scale (its assessment diagnostic). Both are retained here as phase-appropriate options; the fuller skill and the objective require the child to construct the scale.

The optional on-screen mechanics (draggable ruler, X snapping to the measured value, live recompute, flagging a mis-positioned X or skipped scale value) are preserved as example interaction mechanisms, not mandatory requirements; the same objective can be met with physical ruler, objects, and paper.
The ~20% figure and bar-graph transfer claim derive from a single cited study (Kaplan et al. 2014) applied here to a grade-2 line-plot context; not independently re-verified.
