learn.summary: Children generate measurement data by measuring objects to the nearest half inch and to the nearest quarter inch on a ruler whose subdivisions they can read and name, then display the data on a line plot whose horizontal scale is partitioned into equal quarter-inch intervals (…2, 2¼, 2½, 2¾, 3…). The demanding new skill is the SCALE: equal spacing, correct fraction ordering (2¼ < 2½ < 2¾), and recognising that 2½ sits at the same position as 2 2/4 (because ½ = 2/4). A guiding practice is drawing the axis to true inch scale and keeping the ruler's quarter-inch ticks aligned with the plot's quarter marks so the subdivision of the tool and the subdivision of the axis are seen as the same partition of one unit. activities.title: Measure to the nearest quarter and build the fractional scale
feedback: If the quarter marks are unevenly spaced or out of order (e.g. 2¼, 2¾, 2½): reteach partitioning one unit into equal parts with a fraction strip; align each ¼ tick under the ruler and check the order 2¼ < 2½ < 2¾.

If the child records a tick position like 'the third line' but cannot name the fraction it represents: label the quarter ticks with their fraction values and practise naming ¼, ½, ¾ on the ruler before plotting.
If the child answers 'how long is one?' with a stack's count: align the ruler under the plot and separate 'how many objects' (stack height) from 'how long is one object' (axis position).

activities.rationale: The grade-level objective is to generate measurement data with a ruler marked in halves and fourths and display it on a line plot scaled appropriately. Building the equal-interval fractional scale is a construction skill, so the activity has learners physically measure, partition, and place marks rather than only interpret a given plot. Aligning the ruler under the axis is intended to make the shared subdivision concrete.
sourceClaims: Grade 3 standard: generate measurement data by measuring lengths using rulers marked with halves and fourths of an inch; show the data by making a line plot where the horizontal scale is marked off in appropriate units — whole numbers, halves, or quarters.
learnerActions: Measure a set of ribbons or objects (about 5–6) against a ruler whose quarter-inch ticks are clearly marked and, at first, labelled with their fraction values (¼, ½, ¾).

For each object, name the quarter inch it rounds to out loud or in writing — e.g. 'this one is 2¾ inches', not 'the third line'; for one or two objects, also name the nearest half inch and notice that the two answers can be different.

Using the ruler to mark it, draw a number line at true scale (1 inch per whole number) that covers every measured length, and partition it into equal quarters between the whole numbers, so the marks run e.g. 2, 2¼, 2½, 2¾, 3 in correct order and with equal spacing.
Place one X per object at its fractional value on the line.

Align the ruler directly under the true-scale plot, with the ruler's whole-inch marks under the matching whole numbers on the axis, so each ¼ tick on the ruler sits beneath the matching ¼ mark on the axis.
(Optional, on screen) Measure a ribbon that is 2¼ inches: drop its X and watch it settle one quarter-tick past 2, directly beneath the same tick on the ruler, making the shared subdivision visible.
Check ordering and equivalence explicitly: confirm 2¼ < 2½ < 2¾, and that 2½ lands at the same position as 2 2/4 (because ½ = 2/4).
Read the finished plot: e.g. 'how many objects were 2½ inches?' and 'how many were shorter than 2½?'
activities.intendedInsight: The subdivision on the ruler and the subdivision on the plot's axis are the same partition of one unit into equal quarters; a measured length maps to a position on an equal-interval scale, and ½ = 2/4 is one position, not two.

activities.title: Separate frequency from length
feedback: If the child reads stack height as length: physically align the ruler under the plot, then ask them to trace the axis position for length and separately count Xs for frequency, naming which answers which question.
Reinforce with the probe 'How many objects were shorter than 2½? How can you tell?' so counting across stacks is tied to axis position.
activities.rationale: Research reports that students transfer a bar-graph habit of reading bar/stack height as a data value, confusing frequency with the value of the variable on the axis, and this confusion can persist after instruction even in simple dot plots. Explicitly separating the two questions aims to address this documented error; its effectiveness here is not independently established.
sourceClaims: Students transfer the bar-graph habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (stack height) with the value of the variable (axis position); the axis confusion persists after instruction and appears even in simple dot plots.
learnerActions: On a completed fractional line plot, point to the axis position that gives an object's LENGTH and separately count the stacked Xs that give the FREQUENCY at that length.
Answer paired questions: 'How long is this object?' (read axis) versus 'How many objects were this long?' (count the stack).
Explain in your own words why a taller stack does not mean a longer object.
activities.intendedInsight: On a line plot the horizontal axis position is the measured value, while the height of a stack of Xs is how many objects share that value — these are two different quantities.

activities.title: Interpret and order a given fractional plot
feedback: If ordering is wrong, return to a fraction strip to compare ¼, ½, ¾ as equal parts of one unit.
If the child treats ½ and 2/4 as different positions, mark both on the same strip and show they coincide.
activities.rationale: Reading a given plot tests interpretation, ordering, and equivalence. It is a useful complement to construction, though on its own it does not show whether a child can build a correctly spaced quarter scale from scratch — so it should accompany, not replace, the measuring-and-plotting task.
learnerActions: Given a finished fractional line plot, order the marked values 2¼, 2½, 2¾ from least to greatest.
Count how many objects fall at a given value (e.g. 'how many were 2½?').
Compare: how many objects were shorter than 2½, and how many were longer.
Confirm that 2½ and 2 2/4 name the same position on the scale (because ½ = 2/4).
activities.intendedInsight: A correctly built fractional scale can be read for order, counts, and comparisons, and equivalent fractions occupy the same position.

activities.title: Reference: name each quarter mark and show ½ = 2/4
feedback: If the child cannot name a tick, return to the labelled reference and say the value aloud before plotting.
Fade the labels once the child reliably names and orders the quarters without them.
activities.rationale: A labelled reference scaffolds correct naming and ordering of quarter marks and makes the ½ = 2/4 equivalence explicit. It is a support, not a substitute for measuring to the nearest quarter or constructing the scale, so it is faded as competence grows.
learnerActions: Study a labelled fractional line plot or fraction strip where each quarter mark is named (¼, ½, ¾).
Reveal or confirm that ½ equals 2/4 and that the half mark sits midway between adjacent whole numbers.
Use this as a reference while measuring and plotting, then set it aside once the scale can be built independently.
activities.intendedInsight: Each quarter tick has a nameable fraction value, and equivalent fractions (½ = 2/4) share one position; this naming supports accurate measuring and plotting.

constraints: Use a ruler with clearly marked quarter-inch subdivisions, labelled at first, so children can name the fraction value of the tick they round to rather than recording 'the nearest line'.
Keep the ruler's ¼-inch tick spacing aligned with the plot's ¼ spacing so the tool and the axis share one subdivision.
Maintain the one-X-per-object rule established with whole-unit plots.
Check ordering and equivalence explicitly: 2¼ < 2½ < 2¾, and 2½ at the same position as 2 2/4 (because ½ = 2/4).

A labelled reference image or tap-to-reveal plot is a scaffold for naming marks; being fixed, it does not by itself exercise measuring to the nearest quarter or constructing the scale, so pair it with hands-on measuring and plotting and fade it.

Reading-only tasks (ordering, counting on a given plot) assess interpretation but do not show whether a child can build a correctly spaced, correctly ordered quarter scale; include a construction task to cover that.

Snap-to-equal-spacing or tick-alignment feedback (whether on screen or via physically aligning a ruler under the plot) is an optional way to make the shared subdivision visible; it is not the only way to teach equal intervals.

The original claim that a static picture or quiz 'cannot deliver' the insight has been softened: a fixed reference can still teach naming and equivalence; it simply cannot be manipulated to practise measuring or building the scale. Example values (2, 2¼, 2½, 2¾, 3) and the equivalence ½ = 2/4 were checked and are correct; ordering 2¼ < 2½ < 2¾ is correct.

pedagogy.summary: This extends line plots to eighth-inch precision and, crucially, USES the plotted data for computation — finding the difference between the longest and shortest specimen, or totalling all the measurements — which requires adding and subtracting fractions with like and related denominators. Two skills are fused: build an accurate 1/8 scale, and operate on the fractions read from it. It is best taught by generating data, plotting to the nearest 1/8, then posing genuine questions answerable only from the plot (difference, total, redistribution), with the eighth scale showing equivalence (2/8 = ¼, 4/8 = ½) so common denominators are visible on the axis itself.
bestPractices: Measure to the nearest 1/8 inch with a subdivided ruler and scale the axis into equal eighths
Make equivalence visible on the scale — mark that 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½ — so common denominators for later arithmetic are seen, not just computed
Pose real difference and total problems that can only be answered by reading positions and adding fractions
Stress that a stack of Xs contributes its value once per X (three Xs at 3/8 add 3/8 three times) — multiplicity matters when totalling
Keep the one-X-per-case rule and connect eighths back to quarters and halves

A number line in eighths showing equivalence (2/8 = ¼, 4/8 = ½)
Fraction bars for adding and subtracting like denominators

learn.summary: Grade 4 measurement line plots at eighth-inch precision, fused with using the plotted data for fraction arithmetic. Learners measure specimens to the nearest 1/8 inch, build an equal-interval eighth scale, plot one X per object, then answer genuine questions that require adding and subtracting fractions with like/related denominators: the difference between longest and shortest, and the total length of everything. The key insight comes when totalling over stacks: three Xs at 3/8 contribute 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8, so frequency (how many Xs) and value (how much length) diverge. Marking 2/8 = 1/4 and 4/8 = 1/2 on the axis makes common denominators visible, so 1/2 − 3/8 becomes 4/8 − 3/8 right on the scale.

activities.title: Build-then-compute an eighth-inch line plot
feedback: If the learner gives the number of objects as the 'total', point to a stack of three at 3/8 and ask 'how much length is here?', holding 'how many objects' apart from 'how much length'.
If the learner adds each distinct axis value only once while ignoring stack height, show that each X on the stack contributes its value again (three Xs at 3/8 give 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 = 9/8).
If the learner writes 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/16, reteach fraction addition as joining same-size parts: the denominator (the size of the part) stays the same, so 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/8.
If ticks are mis-spaced or 1/2 − 3/8 is attempted without a common denominator, overlay quarter and half ticks on the eighth scale and use a fraction strip to find the common denominator (1/2 = 4/8).
activities.rationale: The standard asks learners both to make a line plot in fractions of a unit and to solve addition/subtraction problems using that plot, so building and computing should be fused rather than separated. Posing a total over stacked Xs directly targets the documented frequency-vs-value confusion.

learnerActions: Measure several real objects (e.g. seedlings or paper strips) to the nearest 1/8 inch using a ruler subdivided into eighths; include some objects that share a length.
Draw a number line marked in equally spaced intervals that each represent 1/8 inch, and plot one X per object at its measured value.
Mark where 2/8 lines up with 1/4 and where 4/8 lines up with 1/2 directly on the axis.
Find longest − shortest by subtracting the two fractional positions, converting to a common denominator on the scale (e.g. 1/2 − 3/8 = 4/8 − 3/8 = 1/8).
Find the total length of all objects by adding each object's value with multiplicity — a stack of three Xs at 3/8 contributes 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 = 9/8, not '3'.
Predict how the total changes if one more object at 1/2 is added, then check (the total rises by 1/2 = 4/8).
activities.intendedInsight: An accurate eighth scale makes equivalences (2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2) and common denominators visible, and totalling over a plot means summing measured values with multiplicity — which is different from counting Xs.

activities.title: Compute from a given plot: difference and total
feedback: If the answer equals the count of Xs, revisit the distinction between how many Xs and how much length.
If a non-standard sum appears (e.g. denominators added, giving 6/16), reteach that same-size parts are joined with the denominator unchanged, so 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/8.
Confirm correct work by checking the common-denominator conversion against the axis ticks (e.g. 1/2 reads as 4/8).

As a reference it does not exercise measuring to the nearest 1/8 or performing the computations independently, so it supports rather than replaces the main activity.

constraints: Learners must construct the scale themselves and measure to the nearest 1/8 inch; a given-plot or tap-to-reveal task isolates computation or shows equivalence but does not exercise building an accurate eighth scale or measuring.
Scale-building should be assessed through actual construction; recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of an equal-interval scale.
Keep the one-X-per-case convention, and ensure eighth intervals are drawn equally spaced so quarter/half ticks line up.
The total must be computed by summing measured values with multiplicity, not by counting Xs; keep frequency and value explicitly distinct.

An interactive panel showing live arithmetic (e.g. selecting a stack to lay out 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8) or overlaying quarter/half ticks is an optional way to make the mechanism concrete, not a required tool; the same reasoning can be done with a ruler, drawn number line and fraction strips.

assess.correctAnswer: Builds an equal-interval eighth-inch scale, plots one X per object, finds longest − shortest by subtracting the two fractional positions over a common denominator, and totals by adding each object's value WITH multiplicity (a stack of three at 3/8 contributes 3/8 three times), recognising 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½.

errorPatterns.pattern: When asked for total length, adds or counts the Xs (frequency) instead of summing the measured values
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to a stack of three at 3/8 and ask 'how much length is here?'; hold apart 'how many objects' from 'how much length'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the number of objects as the 'total', or adds each distinct axis value once while ignoring stack height

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds fractions by adding numerators and denominators (3/8 + 3/8 = 6/16)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach fraction addition as joining same-size parts using fraction bars, denominator unchanged
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Non-standard sums when totalling or differencing the measurements

errorPatterns.pattern: Spaces eighths unequally or doesn't see 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½, so scales don't line up and common denominators are missed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay quarter and half ticks on the eighth scale to show equivalence; use a fraction strip to find the common denominator
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Mis-spaced ticks, or subtracting ½ − 3/8 without converting to a common denominator

responseLevels.gap: Cannot build an accurate eighth scale or cannot operate on the fractions; totals by counting Xs or adds denominators.
responseLevels.full: Builds an equal-interval eighth scale showing equivalence, plots one X per case, and computes both difference and total correctly — summing values with multiplicity and using common denominators — transferring to an added data point.
responseLevels.partial: Builds and reads the plot and can do one operation (e.g. the difference) but mishandles multiplicity in totals or needs prompting to find a common denominator; lists values without combining them correctly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a ruler marked in eighths and several objects, some sharing a length. Say: 'Measure each to the nearest eighth inch, plot them, then tell me the difference between the longest and shortest, and the total length of all of them.' Watch the scale-building, and especially watch how they handle stacks of more than one X when totalling, and how they subtract the two fractional positions.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking for a TOTAL over stacks forces the child to separate frequency (count of Xs) from value (length) AND to add fractions correctly. A child running the bar-graph habit totals by counting Xs; a child adding numerators and denominators produces a specific wrong sum. Each error shows a different, diagnosable signature in both the plot and the arithmetic — which asking about the procedure would not reveal.

sources.claim: Grade 4 standard: make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8); solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 4.MD.B.4

sources.claim: Students transfer the bar-graph habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (count / stack height) with the value of the variable; the confusion persists after instruction and appears in dot plots. This underlies totalling a plot by counting Xs rather than summing values.
sources.source: Kaplan, Gabrosek, Curtiss & Malone (2014), 'Investigating Student Understanding of Histograms', Journal of Statistics Education 22(2)
